#739. Hearts' European hopes hang by a thread but Vrancken proud

Hearts' hopes of a memorable draw with Monaco were dashed in the 94th minute

There was a bittersweet feeling at Tynecastle after Folarin Balogun's 94th-minute winner preserved Monaco's perfect Conference League record and condemned Hearts to a third defeat from four.

Wouter Vrancken's side had gone toe-to-toe with one of the best teams in the tournament, scored two glorious goals, but ultimately came away with nothing for their efforts.

Now they have little to no margin for error in their two remaining league phase matches.

They will likely have to beat both Borac Banja Luka of Bosnia and Cyprus' Pafos to reach the knockout stages, but if they perform as they did against Monaco, they will give themselves a fighting chance.

Hearts have garnered a reputation as entertainers under Vrancken - scoring a raft of goals while being porous at the back.

This game was their season in microcosm. The goals - scored by Jordi Altena and Sabah Kerjota - were things of beauty, picture-perfect strikes worthy of any stage.

But as thrilling as Hearts were in attack, they were as baffling at the back.

Jamie McCart unnecessarily tripped Matthis Abline, allowing Balogun to score from the penalty spot and Monaco's second came from Altena giving the ball away.

"It's Gladiators - are we not entertained? It's sensational," said Hearts legend John Robertson at half-time, with the game finely poised at 2-2.

Monaco strike in 94th minute to break Hearts in five-goal epic

Latest Hearts news, analysis and fan views

Both teams had chances to win it in the second half, but it was Monaco who took theirs in the final stages. Mamadou Coulibaly was afforded too much space and he slipped Balogun through to beat Beau Reus.

"It's a lack of nous and a little bit of naivety," former Hearts midfielder Michael Stewart said on TNT Sports. "McCart backs off and allows the ball to be played into Balogun's feet."

Despite the frustrating nature of the late concession, Vrancken's overwhelming emotion was of pride.

"I'm very disappointed with how we give the goal away at the end," he said.

"The biggest thing is the pride for the performance today. Against a side of Monaco's [quality] - we're still missing nine players through injury - this performance was really pleasing."

Before the recent international break, Hearts were beaten 3-1 by Swiss outfit Thun, before a shock 5-2 home defeat by high-flying Falkirk in the Scottish Premiership.

However, they bounced back with a ruthless 8-0 win at Dundee on Saturday and carried that confidence into this game against a team with a far bigger budget.

"You saw that the confidence was there from the weekend and there was conviction around their box," Vrancken added. "It will not work every time, but the conviction and energy was there again.

"Our team kept their heads in the game and kept going for it, not being pleased with 2-2. Really pleased with what I saw."

Aside from his dismay at Balogun's winner and how it came about, Vrancken's main gripe was with the officials.

He felt there was a foul on Kerjota in the build-up to Monaco's second goal and was bemused at the fact neither Takumi Minamino and Denis Zakaria were sent off.

Minamino - already on a yellow card - wiped out Sabri Guendouz on the edge of the Monaco box, but got away with a warning. And VAR opted not to intervene after Zakaria went over the top of the ball and caught Pierre Landry Kabore on the shin.

"The second goal, they pulled Sabah [Kerjota] and he can't do his defensive work," Vrancken said.

"It was not the only refereeing decision that was interesting tonight. I don't know how it's possible not to give a red card for the tackle on [Pierre Landry Kabore]. It's clearly above the ankle, so it's always a red card.

"And why didn't Minamino get a second yellow before half-time? He prevents a shot from Sabri at the edge of the box.

"The explanation of the fourth official was even more crazy - he explained it could be for his first yellow card, but not for his second yellow. It was clearly a yellow card and then we were against 10 in the second half."

Tyson Fury's manager Spencer Brown revealed Anthony Joshua called him to check if their fight was still going ahead, after claims the 'Gypsy King' had been diagnosed with schizophrenia.

Paris Fury made the claims during a new Netflix documentary about her husband's life, but later retracted her comments, clarifying: "[Fury] doesn't have this condition and has never received a diagnosis."

While some had raised questions over whether the 38-year-old would be able to fight, the British Boxing Board of Control [BBBoC], on Friday, announced it had cleared Fury, adding he had passed pre-fight tests.

Speaking to Dev Sahni, Brown flatly dismissed claims that their December 11 fight was in jeopardy.

"Even Anthony Joshua rang me and said: 'Is this fight going on, because I've heard rumours that his licence…" Brown said.

"I said: 'One-million per cent [the fight is on], just turn up and be there. The fight's happening; it's unbelievable'."

Fury posted on Instagram on Friday night to explain how delighted he was about the launch of his new documentary TYSON FURY, urging fans to watch the film, before adding: "The journey continues, next stop December 11."

Netflix says it has worked to "update" the footage in light of Paris' clarification on Thursday.

The documentary explores Fury's experiences with depression, anxiety and bipolar disorder after they became acute following his 2015 world championship victory over Wladimir Klitschko.

Brown said the 38-year-old was more focused on his training rather than speculation about the fight.

"To him, it's a load of old rubbish from 10 years ago," Brown said.

"Obviously, it's reared its head. People have decided to make an issue of it, when there is no issue. And people panicked a little bit. So, there is no issue. The fight goes on."

Brown added: "It's been noted and everybody knows that Tyson has suffered from a mental illness. And we all know that. It's out everywhere.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"That was a long time ago, he's very happy, and I've never seen him in a better headspace, to be quite honest."

Fury's manager also revealed the lengths his team are going to to help the Wythenshawe-born fighter prepare for the bout.

"I speak to him nearly every day," he said.

"Some mundane things about, we have to make sure that he's travelled right and he's in his hotel and that wherever he's staying, every minute thing has to be done right, down to the windows being blacked out.

"Because he's on a different sleep pattern because they're fighting late at night.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"We have to make sure that he's got solitude, and he's happy, and he's smiling every day. His food is there, transport is there.

"His security are there. Everything has to be done to a specification."

Brown also issued a warning to Joshua ahead of the fight.

"If you're listening, Anthony Joshua, the fight's on," Brown said. "Get ready. Make sure that chin of yours is solid. Because it's going to need to be."

If you've been affected by anything discussed in this article, support is available; please visit Sky Viewer Support.

If you are worried about your mental health, get advice and support through your GP or call the NHS on 111.

#737. Russia strikes Zelenskyy's hometown, killing 2

The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea.

Russian  ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine's southern city of Kryvyi Rih — President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown — killed two people and wounded dozens of others, local officials said Saturday.

The attacks come amid little progress in talks to end the nearly five-year-old war and after Ukraine, on three occasions this week, struck the Kerch bridge linking Russian-occupied Crimea with Russia.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had vowed a "painful" response to the Kerch attack, as the bridge is vital for war supplies for Russian forces in the south.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Among the dead in Friday evening's double-tap strikes on Kryvyi Rih were a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, while several children were among the 60 wounded, the Ukrainian officials said.

Several fires broke out and damage was caused to about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram.

Moscow, meanwhile, confirmed a further strike on Friday night in Kryvyi Rih.

Russia's Defense Ministry said a thermal power plant in the city was hit, along with a power substation in the region of Rivne, on the opposite side of the country.

Both facilities supply electricity to the industry supporting Ukraine's military, the ministry added.

Elsewhere in the nearly five-year-long war, Russia ​also struck a ​cargo vessel ‌near Odesa, which Moscow said was carrying dual-use goods ​for ⁠the Ukrainian military.

Eleven people, including two children, were wounded when a Russian drone attacked a five-story apartment building in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Saturday.

One person was wounded in a Russian attack on the capital, Kyiv, according to the service.

In Russia, local officials said Saturday that Ukrainian drone attacks wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions.

Finland, meanwhile, said it detected a drone attack on Saturday morning on a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea, prompting Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to warn that the war is "spilling over into our immediate vicinity."

After damage to Russia's Kerch bridge to Crimea, Zelenskyy warned in an interview with US broadcaster NBC that the structure "will not remain standing anyway."

#736. Lammens - the Man Utd goalkeeper under scrutiny like never before

Senne Lammens (left) joined Manchester United in the summer of 2025

After a first season at Manchester United that drew little but praise, goalkeeper Senne Lammens is under the microscope like never before.

A bad mistake that gifted Sporting their second goal on Wednesday, having earlier conceded a clumsy penalty, followed several other errors so far this season.

The 24-year-old Belgium international also made an error at the World Cup in the summer, spilling a shot that led to Spain's winning goal in the 88th minute of their quarter-final.

"I don't know [at what point Manchester United drop him]," legendary Manchester United goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel told CBS Sports on Wednesday.

"Mauricio Pochettino has come in and brought his own staff. That means he's got a new goalkeeping coach and maybe that is something that can change it for him.

"[At the World Cup] he came on against Spain and made a bit of a mistake. Mikel Merino scored and they got knocked out. I feel he's lost a little bit of confidence from that mistake and hasn't really recovered.

"As a goalkeeper, when you're not on your best form, you need your defenders in front of you to help you out. The sad truth is that they haven't been able to do that and that makes it so much worse. I like him a lot but today was not a great day for him."

Director of football Jason Wilcox and United's data team overruled Ruben Amorim when they opted to sign Lammens from Royal Antwerp for Â£18.1m in September 2025.

Amorim wanted Argentina World Cup winner Emiliano Martinez, who was left waiting for a deadline day call that never came to seal a move from Aston Villa.

United felt Lammens had the attributes to become one of the world's best goalkeepers. At 24, he is still young. Schmeichel was 27 when he joined United in 1991. Edwin van der Sar was 34 when he left Fulham in 2005. Both had hundreds of senior appearances behind them. Lammens has just over 100, more than half of them with Royal Antwerp.

Although he made the odd error last season, Lammens did nothing to suggest Wilcox and co had got it wrong.

After releasing Turkey international Altay Bayindir, who replaced Andre Onana as first choice at the start of last season and is back on loan in Turkey with Trabzonspor, they signed 36-year-old Wales international Karl Darlow as back-up this term.

Darlow finished last season as first choice at Leeds. But he only started 30 league games in three seasons with the Elland Road outfit. Also on the bench in Lisbon was Tom Heaton. The 40-year-old has not played in a senior game since February 2023.

Mistakes earlier in the season â former United midfielder Paul Scholes claimed in September '"the jury is still out" on whether Lammens is truly top class â have brought increased analysis. His positioning for Dominik Szoboszlai's opening goal for Liverpool on Sunday was questioned externally, even if United focused their attentions on Bradley Barcola shoving into the wall.

Just 75 seconds after getting down to make an excellent save from Luis Suarez's first penalty, Lammens recklessly charged out and upended Maxi Araujo, even though Noussair Mazraoui seemed to be in a position to deal with it.

Then, after two Bruno Fernandes goals at the start of the second period had turned the Champions League tie in the visitors' favour, Lammens reached to collect a high ball and inexplicably dropped it in front of Suarez, who applied the overhead kick finish.

Understandably, there was sympathy in the dressing room.

"This team is a family," said striker Joshua Zirkzee. "There's no-one who will suffer by themselves.

"Senne is a great goalkeeper and mistakes happen. In this moment, we just give him space. I'm not sure if he wants to hear anything at all. But Senne's a great kid. He's got a good head on him. We didn't draw because of him, and we all know that next game he is going to be at the top of his game."

'One mistake from being dropped' - Ashley Young on Senne Lammens

Toni Jimenez is Pochettino's long-time goalkeeping coach.

His arrival triggered the exit of Craig Mawson, who had been with Manchester United since 2019. Connor King is Jimenez's assistant but a relative newcomer himself, having joined from Burnley in 2026.

By its nature, goalkeeping at the highest level can be a mental challenge as well as a technical one. As Onana discovered, flaws can quickly become major issues and once the spotlight is shining, the attention is fierce.

Lammens has given the impression privately of being strong. He has seemed remarkably unaffected by his World Cup torment â his mistake against Spain came after he was introduced as a 71st-minute replacement for injured veteran Thibaut Courtois with the quarter-final delicately poised at 1-1. But only he knows the full picture.

Jimenez will be Pochettino's guide over what to do about the situation, although for now, Lammens' head coach is behind him.

"This type of thing happens," he said. "That is football. Football is about making mistakes.

"I always want to support my player. I think we need to talk about responsibility. In this type of action our defensive line needs to cover the keeper better because it was very difficult.

"It's not to blame the defensive line, but it's two things that we need to improve, details that we need to work on. We need to manage his type of situation better."

Following Wednesday's draw in Lisbon, Pochettino highlighted "two things" that need to improve if United are to start winning matches on a regular basis.

The first of those is the club's preferred goalkeeper. Of the 17 Premier League goalkeepers to have played a minimum of 10 matches in all competitions in this campaign, Lammens has the second-worst save success rate, keeping out just 60.2% of the shots he has faced. Only Coventry's Carl Rushworth (54.4%) has fared worse so far this season.

Lammens also ranks bottom of those 17 goalkeepers for clean sheet ratio (6.3%).

And there is substance to the suggestion that Lammens has declined in 2026-27. He made just one error leading to a goal in the entirety of last season in contrast to two already in this campaign. The data also shows that he is currently preventing far fewer goals.

The second "thing", however, has significant bearing on the first.

Clean sheets and conceding fewer goals are clearly a collective responsibility, particularly for the "defensive line" that Pochettino referenced on Wednesday - and United's defence has collectively struggled this season.

They have now let in 36 goals in all competitions, the most of any team in Europe's top five leagues. They have also conceded five penalties and received five red cards - both the second-highest tallies among Europe's elite divisions.

So is Lammens more error-prone this season? Apparently yes. But he's also playing behind a defence that, on current form, may not inspire too much confidence in their goalkeeper.

#734. Don't sleep on the NFL 'uncs' - can they finally win a Super Bowl?

We preview Sunday in Week 12 of the 2026 NFL season as the San Francisco 49ers face the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks live on Sky Sports from 9.25pm; also watch New York Giants vs Indianapolis Colts and Atlanta Falcons against Minnesota Vikings

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Kyle Shanahan's San Francisco 49ers are the best team in football. Is this finally the season they win a Lombardi Trophy? Their next test is against the champions.

Most offenses in the NFL look and function the way they do because of the Shanahan. His fingerprints, and still that of his father, have long been ingrained in trends, wrinkles and schematic interpretations dominant across the league as fans know it.

He tops the tree that has shaped modern football. And he is beating them all at his own game. He has done so for some time, minus the shiny reward at the end.

In that sense he sits alongside Josh Allen, even Joe Burrow and Lamar Jackson, in likely believing he would have a ring were it not for Patrick Mahomes, Andy Reid and the Kansas City Chiefs' Super Bowl dynasty, which twice have taken down Shanahan's 49ers in the season finale.

But the Niners look good for another Championship run. And few deserve it quite like Shanahan.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

It would be a staggering case study were he not to win a Super Bowl at some stage in San Francisco, bearing in mind not only the number of close calls for a team he has led to four NFC Championship Games - two of which he won - in nine seasons, but also the genius football brain that has governed sidelines and film rooms across the nation.

His 49ers sit 9-1 in pole position for the No 1 seed in the NFC heading into Sunday night's matchup with the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks. They do so having just dismantled the Minnesota Vikings and their league-leading scoring defense 35-10 in Mexico City; only twice this season had teams put up more than 20 points against Brian Flores' defense. Shanahan torched them with ease.

It was a message to teams across the league, many of which had been foiled by Flores, his blitz bombardments and camouflaged coverages. It, too, was further evidence of an expertly drilled operation that stormed past the Los Angeles Rams in Melbourne, Australia in kickoff week before making Mexico home in famously tricky high-altitude conditions. Should they win a Super Bowl, the NFL's 'are they really world champions?' debate loses some substance; the Niners have gone global.

Shanahan's offense entered Week 12 ranked second in yards per game, sixth in passing, fourth in rushing and No 1 in scoring while topping all teams in EPA/play and success rate as the most prolific attack in football.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

At the heart of it is Brock Purdy, who Shanahan both identified and cultivated from Mr Irrelevant to undeniable MVP candidate. Non-Purdy believers had deemed him the product of the Shanahan system; to admit that could be partly true would be a deserved nod to what San Francisco's head coach does as one of football's masterminds. Nonetheless, Purdy has proven he is more than a mere puppet surrounded by stars.

Purdy is 206 of 290 passing (71 per cent) for 2,624 yards and 23 touchdowns to just five interceptions with a league-high passer rating of 118.2. It should be noted he has missed practice this week due to an ankle issue. So stay tuned.

He is wildly accurate, underrated as a creator outside of the pocket, clinical in decision-making, aggressive enough to attack downfield and an outstanding diagnostician. The win over Minnesota in Mexico was the newest addition to his MVP resume, behind which Shanahan has been phenomenal.

Purdy was 16 of 18 for 195 yards and two touchdowns when facing the blitz, while finishing eight of nine for 100 yards when pressured during blitzes, according to NextGen Stats. It would contribute to an offensive display that saw the Vikings managed an EPA per dropback of 0.613; no other team had surpassed 0.037 EPA per dropback against Minnesota entering Week 11, per Pro Football Focus. His head coach is putting him in positions for success, and Purdy is executing.

"He's the best player in the game right now. He's super dialled in, the way he prepares, the way he competes," said wide receiver Mike Evans. "He's tough. I always thought he's been underrated, his precision. Super smart player."

Purdy may not win MVP with Joe Burrow around. And Shanahan probably will not win Coach of the Year. That doesn't mean he isn't the best coach in the NFL.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

In many ways he and Purdy are a match made in heaven, perfectly suited to one another. They are also thriving together in the face of seemingly never-ending injury obstacles.

They lead an old guard of veteran weapons, who sense another championship campaign.

George Kittle has been Purdy's most targeted pass catcher with 47 catches for a team-high 591 and seven touchdowns, while Christian McCaffrey has over 1,000 yards from scrimmage with a second-most 14 total touchdowns. Mike Evans is the big-bodied one-on-one target Purdy and Shanahan have been missing, but has missed time through injury, and Deebo Samuel is channelling his wide back days again, but has missed time through injury.

"You have to at some point put Purdy in the MVP conversation with what he's been able to do for this 49ers team," said Sky Sports NFL's Phoebe Schecter.

"I think it's hard not to look at what happened in Mexico City and not feel like this team is unstoppable, even with a litany of injuries that are going on."

The next test comes against the champions, whose defense leads the NFL in yards allowed and passing while ranking fourth in scoring and second in pressure rate.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"This Seattle defense have been so fun to watch all season long, and I think you couldn't ask for someone better in terms of Mike Macdonald," said Schecter. "They are gonna come after Brock Purdy. I know we saw the Vikings come with what felt like 90 per cent blitz rate, but I think this Seahawks team will come with a different attitude because Purdy picked them apart."

"This is a battle where the NFC West is kind of in the hands of Seattle and San Francisco."

Is this finally Shanahan's time? With the Seahawks, Los Angeles Rams and Chiefs coming up over the next month, their Super Bowl credentials are about to be put to the test.

Mike Evans is 33. Keenan Allen is 34. They are two of the NFL's greatest wide receivers, and now find themselves with instrumental roles to play in San Francisco's Super Bowl hunt. Evans arrived in the offseason and Allen more recently ahead of the trade deadline, playing 19 snaps together in the 49ers' 35-10 win over the Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City. Behold the "unc package".

"We mix in so many guys, and I know everybody's name, but when I'm thinking about football and stuff, I don't always just spit out names fast. So sometimes it's just easier for me to say unc," said head coach Shanahan. "Everyone knows who I'm talking about. "I hope they like it. I think it's cool. They're not, like, really uncles. They're in their 30s. They're still young."

The nickname stemmed from George Kittle as he declared the 49ers' veteran-heavy offense "Unc city", the criteria for which is being over the age of 30. Evans is in his 13th season and Allen his 14th, both still one-on-one headaches for defenders across the league and crucial pairs of hands for Purdy come January playoff football.

Sleep is a sensitive subject in the NFL this week. But don't sleep on those uncs. Kittle, for the record, insisted he is not part of 'Unc city', despite being 33.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The state of things in the NFC East. No, quite literally - the state of things!

The truly dreadful standard of the NFC South is letting the East off the hook a little, but the 'battle' for supremacy among four of the NFL's most storied franchises isn't much better.

The New York Giants (6-3-1) hold the advantage, having secured arguably the best win of their season over the Jacksonville Jaguars last week, but their schedule down the stretch - following a winnable trip to the Indianapolis Colts this Sunday - looks rough, and so they could conceivably still be caught.

Whether the Dallas Cowboys (5-7), Washington Commanders (4-5-1) and Philadelphia Eagles (4-7) are capable of chasing the Giants down, though, is another matter entirely!

The Commanders could gain some ground with wins against the lowly Arizona Cardinals and Tennessee Titans over the next two weeks, plus they hold the head-to-head tiebreaker with New York.

As for the Cowboys, a season already rich with embarrassing lows reached a new nadir when blowing a Thanksgiving-record 21-point lead (with little more than a quarter left) to the Eagles, who are surely already out of contention despite that stunning comeback.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Kirk Cousins doesn't exactly scream somebody who chases revenge, but how he would love to stick it to the franchise that cast him aside as he leads the Minnesota Vikings (7-3) out against the Atlanta Falcons (3-7) this weekend. Cousins signed a bumper four-year $180m deal with Atlanta in 2024 after six seasons in Minnesota, only to see the Falcons go and select another quarterback in Michael Penix Jr with the eighth overall pick in the Draft that same year. Cousins was benched ahead of Week 16 before beginning the 2025 season as backup and starting just eight games until he was released this past offseason. He has since prolonged his days as a starter in the NFL with the Las Vegas Raiders, and recently returned to the Vikings via a trade in a bid to ignite Kevin O'Connell's slumping offense. Once deemed something of a final piece route back to prominence for the Falcons, Cousins is now intent on plunging Kevin Stefanski's side further towards trouble.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Sam Darnold has come a long way from "seeing ghosts" during his early struggles with the woeful New York Jets, returning a superb 28-6 record as a starter over the past two seasons which culminated in a Super Bowl ring with the Seattle Seahawks back in February.

As such, you'd have thought his expected return this week for a key NFC West divisional clash with the San Francisco 49ers would be greeted with great fanfare. Not quite…

Darnold has struggled to replicate his championship-winning form of last season, and that of 2024 with the Minnesota Vikings, with his record 3-4 this year. Meanwhile, backup QB Drew Lock has won all three of his starts, in which he's thrown for 837 yards, seven TDs and zero interceptions, completing 73.1 per cent of his passes.

Seattle's playoff hopes, and Darnold's job might both be on the line this Sunday.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

He was the most athletically-gifted quarterback to ever test at the position coming into the NFL, but between persistent accuracy issues and injury setbacks, it has never quite happened for Anthony Richardson since being selected as the fourth pick of the 2023 Draft. He has an arm capable of the otherworldly throws some quarterbacks could only dream of making, and yet an arm prone to botching the most routine plays. At his best there is box office talent, but consistency has tripped him up. Richardson gets a chance to begin rebuilding his career as starter this weekend when he takes the reins for the Indianapolis Colts against the Giants - his first start since the 2024 season. It comes following the release of Daniel Jones amid an outright rebuild in Indianapolis. Awaiting him is a Giants defense ranked seventh in yards and fifth in passing.

#732. Navigating grief in academia: ways to find balance

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Pamela Yeh is a professor of evolutionary biology at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Pamela Yeh with her mother in Los Angeles, California, in the late 1970s.Credit: Courtesy of Pamela Yeh

There are few things in this world that are more universal than grief. And yet, each person’s own particular grief can feel as unique as the person they are grieving for. I have been in academia for decades, but have heard little about grief in that time, so I wanted to share a few tips that helped me get through the early stages of grief when my mother died last year.

My mother grew up in deep poverty in Taiwan and she worked relentlessly throughout her life to give me and my siblings many opportunities. She was the first in her family to go to college, and at 23 years old, she moved to Canada to work as a nurse. After a few years of enduring Canadian winters, she had had enough and moved to sunny California. She met my dad there, and a few years later she gave birth to my sister, then me and then my brother. She raised us while working several jobs as a nurse. She cheered the three of us on throughout our lives. That’s not to say that she ever fully understood my career: she once described my work (I am an evolutionary biologist, specializing in birds and bacteria, at the University of California, Los Angeles) as “counting birds”.

She was adventurous, but between her family and work responsibilities, she didn’t have much time to travel. So, once she retired, I took her on fieldwork and conference trips with me whenever I could — to China, the Netherlands, Italy, Mexico, Japan and throughout the United States.

When her grandchildren came along, she helped them to learn how to read, to do maths and to speak Chinese. In the last years of her life, I had a small house built for her in our back garden in Los Angeles, so she would always be close to me. When you lose someone who is extremely close to you, your world is never the same.

When a loved one dies: how academia can support bereaved colleagues

When a loved one dies: how academia can support bereaved colleagues

In the weeks and months after she died, I found myself in a fog of shock and grief. I felt the need to be moving constantly: running, walking the dog, cleaning the house. At times, I could not be certain of my ability to conduct the high-level abstract and conceptual thinking that academia often requires, so I turned to Trevor Price, my former PhD adviser at the University of California, San Diego (who is now at the University of Chicago, Illinois). I explained my brain fog and deep grief, and he read over my work and made sure that I didn’t miss any crucial scientific arguments in some of the papers I was writing. Although I graduated more than two decades ago, he did not hesitate for one second to help me.

People won’t know that you need help until you reach out. And the earlier you do it, the more time and energy you can give yourself and the easier it will be for others to help.

Here are some tips that helped me to navigate the academic world while grieving.

Ideally, you should determine what support is available before it is needed. Institutions often have all sorts of resources and benefits for people experiencing grief. These might include time off for a bereavement, leave for family care, counselling and a break from teaching classes. I never knew, until my mother passed away, that I could have taken paid leave to take care of her while she was unwell: she had a debilitating stroke five months before she died. Make sure you understand (and ask questions) about your work contract and what your employer offers.

Sometimes, a family member’s illness can occur suddenly, and other times it might start off as one condition and snowball into something else. Talk to the chair of your department and to your colleagues as early as possible about getting cover for your courses and committees. Be creative and brainstorm which other people — including your colleagues, former advisers and former students and postdocs — might be able to step in and give your conference talks, guest lecture for your classes and conduct other activities that you might need help with.

Pamela Yeh (centre) with her parents, husband, son and dog on the front steps of her home in Los Angeles, California, in 2014.Credit: Courtesy of Pamela Yeh

I learnt this the hard way. I did not reach out to people early enough and was unrealistically optimistic about my mother’s health trajectory. While I waited for her to get better, I was so panicked about the thought of losing her that I became incapacitated. I couldn’t focus and, at times, I could barely do simple tasks such as answering e-mails, or making appointments for meetings. I told myself as soon as she was better, which would be any day now, I would catch up. And so, I didn’t have a realistic plan in place when she died.

You have to accept that you might not be at your best when it comes to research productivity, mentoring and teaching while you’re grieving. Ask someone to help with advising your students, and rely on colleagues or former students. You might have to reduce the frequency with which you meet your students, hold laboratory meetings and work with collaborators, and resort to advising through e-mail and video calls. And you might have to give less detailed comments on your students’ writing. I did all of the above during the first few weeks and months of grieving. I had an especially hard time giving advice to my graduate students who were doing field work. Ellie Diamant, a former PhD student of mine who is now a biologist at Bard College in Annandale-On-Hudson, New York, generously stepped in and met with many of my students. It took me a while to understand and accept that I simply wasn’t going to meet the normal standards I set for myself while going through this difficult time.

#726. EU takes aim at tech giants in tax proposal

European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a smaller EU budget for 2028-2034, including a 3% tax on major digital firms to ease member states' contributions. France has already rejected the plan as inadequate.

European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a new draft for the next EU budget.

Among other things, he is suggesting a tax on big tech firms to ease the contributions of member states, some of which strongly criticised earlier proposals.

The EU budget is theEuropean Union’s shared budget and it is used for things ranging from agricultural subsidies, infrastructure projects to border control and defence.

A first draft for the 2028 to 2034 budget was proposed by the EU Commission in 2025 but was criticised, especially by a group of northern European members including Germany who wanted the budget to be much smaller.

Following that criticism, the European Council President has now suggested a new draft, which is smaller by €204 billion.

But divisions among member states appear to remain, with France immediately coming out against Costa’s new draft, saying it was "deeply disappointing."

The proposal includes a string of new "revenue channels," explicitly intended to "to keep national contributions at a reasonable level," so that member state will have to contribute less than otherwise would be the case.

The biggest splash would likely come from a tax on companies with an annual turnover from digital activities of at least 50 million euros in the EU and 750 million euros worldwide.

Those firms would be subject to "an annual contribution corresponding to 3% of the annual net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data," according to Costa.

Aside from the tech tax, the "balanced basket of new own resources" also includes taxes on tobacco products and electronic waste.

Neither the EU Commission nor European Council President Costa will have the final word on the budget. Costa's plan will now be at the centre of hours of talks when EU leaders meet in Brussels next week.

"This is a realistic budget that addresses our new priorities while preserving our established policies," Costa wrote about his proposal. "I am confident that this proposal is a good basis for moving towards a final agreement."

But an initial reaction from France suggests that any final agreement might still be some way off.

The French presidency said the budget "falls well short ​of ‌what is needed, particularly on ‌the Common Agricultural Policy, ‌notably ​to guarantee income support for farmers."

"As it ⁠stands, ​this proposal ​from the President ​of the European ‌Council does not ​provide ⁠a basis for an ⁠agreement."

The EU was hoping to reach a general agreement on the budget by the end of 2026 with its formal adoption planned for 2027.

#724. Nicole Scherzinger, Fiancé Thom Evans Break Up After 7 Years

Nicole Scherzinger’s fiancé Thom Evans announced the couple have broken up seven years after finding love on The X Factor: Celebrity, noting, “This is not the outcome I had ever hoped for.”

Nicole Scherzinger is back to being a solo artist.

Three years after the Pussycat Dolls alum and rugby player Thom Evans became engaged, Evans announced they have broken up.

“It is with a heavy heart that l share that Nicole and l are no longer together,” the 41-year-old wrote in a Nov. 27 Instagram Story. “After seven years of love, commitment and believing in a future together, this is an incredibly difficult time.”

Evans’ statement also seemingly revealed that their parting of ways was not necessarily mutual.

“Whilst this is not the outcome I had ever hoped for,” he wrote, “I respect Nicole's decision and genuinely wish her every happiness in the next chapter of her life.”

Scherzinger, for her part, has not yet addressed their breakup.

Evans and the Broadway star first met in 2019 while filming The X Factor: Celebrity, during which Evans formed part of the boy band Try Star. And though the former professional athlete finished fifth in the competition, he left with an even better prize: Scherzinger’s heart.

Though the pair initially kept their romance buttoned up, they were spotted spending time out and about together in late 2019 before making their red carpet debut as a couple at a Golden Globes after party in Jan. 2020.

Then, three years later, Scherzinger revealed Evans had popped the question in a romantic, beachside proposal.

Alongside photos of Evans down on one knee in the sand before a surprised Scherzinger, the singer captioned her June 2023 post, “I said yes.”

In the time since, the pair have shared the occasional glimpse into their romance on social media.

For his part, Evans showed off his and Scherzinger’s epic summer with a July Instagram dump heavily featuring the singer. He captioned the post, “Lately.”

Meanwhile, the last time Evans appeared on Scherzinger’s Instagram grid was in late September. During a trip to Paris, the then-couple took the time to dance to the music of street performers on the city’s streets.

She wrote over the clip, “Dancing in the city of love with my love,” quipping in the caption, “And getting shown up by the locals.

#723. The local boy aiming to be at the heart of Cardiff's derby aims

Colwill has one goal and three assists from 10 Championship appearances following Cardiff City's return to the Championship

Rubin Colwill is used to being in the centre of things.

He has been the focus of an ongoing argument over his role - or lack of it - in Craig Bellamy's Wales side.

It has meant the midfielder has been the subject of countless questions around international weeks, the latest prompting the Wales boss to ask a journalist if he had a Colwill poster in the middle of his bedroom wall.

The debate has stemmed from the 24-year-old being at the heart of Brian Barry-Murphy's stylish transformation of Cardiff City.

So it is understandable that, as he prepares to lead his boyhood club into the eye of the storm that is the south Wales derby, he is again in the centre of things.

And fitting for someone who grew up in the middle of the rivalry between the two cities.

"I took a lot of stick," Colwill said. Well, we presume that is what he might have said, stopping himself from swearing to describe life as a Cardiff fan from the town of Neath, nine miles from Swansea.

"I probably felt it more than most being surrounded by Swansea fans and a lot of mates being Swansea fans.

"It was tough because they were in the Premier League for a long spell, so I was always trying to give a bit back when we won a game or did well."

Bellamy an influence as Williams leads Swansea

Bellamy jokes reporter has Colwill poster in bedroom

Latest Cardiff City news, analysis and fan views

Colwill was always Cardiff, as was brother Joel, his team-mate for club and country.

Their mother - from Port Talbot, a little further east with a denser amount of support that turn towards the capital - was a Cardiff fan and so were her boys, signing for the club while still in primary school.

He has never gone to a derby in Swansea as a fan - he was never allowed - but was part of the Cardiff side that last won at their rivals in 2021 and has told team-mates all about the journey down the M4, where fans flock to bridges and encouragement turns to abuse as the miles clock up.

He will mention that, and the feeling of the times where, by his own admission, Cardiff were not good enough in a string of defeats that sting more than most.

But he will also share the "no better" feeling of being in the middle of the celebrations of a derby win, as he was in January 2025.

Colwill: 'Tough' growing up as a Cardiff fan

That Cardiff 3-0 victory was a rare high point in a season that eventually saw the club relegated from the Championship and in desperate need of a rebuild.

They have done just that, transitioning into an eye-catching, exciting team, who - depsite failing to win away this season and going into the game on the back of a 4-0 defeat by Preston North End - are ready to show Swansea the Bluebirds are a different beast these days.

Colwill and his influence has been very much a central cog in that change.

He has been game time and responsibility by Barry-Murphy - including the armband that might not be obvious for such a seemingly laidback character.

The academy product says he has learned much from the journey, including a frustrating spell of injuries that have limited his impact to seven starts since the return to the Championship.

It has seemingly been noticed by Bellamy, who spoke before Wales' recent Nations League defeat to Portugal about how he has improved as a player.

"There has been a big change in his game," Bellamy said, a former academy coach of the talented midfielder.

"He is a player I really like watching - before I did and I didn't. Now I see a lot of good things."

Colwill responded with a man-of-the-match performance against Portugal in what was his first competitive Wales start in five years.

"It was almost like I got to experience my first game twice," smiled Colwill.

Bellamy - who has questioned Colwill's work off the ball - has said he felt able to be more "ruthless" with the youngster because of their long association.

"Everyone knows," said Bellamy of what he thought Colwill needed to do to improve. "And none more than him."

Williams to lead Swansea in south Wales derby

Frozen out Robinson told he has Cardiff future

Despite being in the middle of it all, Colwill has not changed in playing personality, and certainly showed no pressure when he reclaimed his Wales spot.

Clearly there is a resilience that goes beyond sticking with a Cardiff scarf in an area full of Swansea colours.

"I've tried to learn from those experiences and develop myself mentally and improve my resilience so I can almost take anything that comes my way," he says.

"I think that's a massive part of football: you've got to stay grounded, stay focused, regardless if you're doing really well or really badly because it's a massive part of the game to stay consistent in the end."

So what of the challenge to improve and being in the middle of the two different approaches to getting the most out of him?

"I think they're very similar," is Colwill's response. "They both want to control the game, the structure, the body shape, how they want us to play, the press and reaction to giving the ball away.

"In the fundamentals of the game, they're similar. Obviously they're both different people so the approaches to that are very different, and it's in the little details.

"With Craig, he's always had that approach of if he thinks you can offer something or improve on, it's on us to take it on board and be open to that constructive criticism.

"It's not always easy. I think he does have a high demand of you, but if you do make a change as he asks of you then he will play you."

Cardiff players will have 'edge' against Swansea

After the stick, the carrot at Cardiff is the chance to follow in Bellamy's footsteps by scoring a winner in the derby at Swansea, as the Wales boss did in 2011 - Cardiff's last win there in front of travelling supporters.

Colwill smiles at the thought, just as he winces at the memories of the defeats - as a player and a fan - which is why he will not be telling team-mates to treat this game like just another.

"That attitude is almost like trying to protect yourself from the pressure," he argues. "But it's not. We have a lot of boys from the area who have come from the academy who really get the game and understand the whole picture of it and how important it is for everyone in the city.

"And we've got no fear of failure - if we lose we just leave it all out there, but we have full belief we can win."

If they do, it will come as no surprise if Colwill is at the heart of it.

#722. Stephen Nedoroscik Debuts New Romance After Tess McCracken Breakup

Olympian Stephen Nedoroscik hard launched a new relationship on Thanksgiving Day, ten months after he and longtime girlfriend Tess McCracken broke up.

Stephen Nedoroscik has a little extra to be thankful for this Thanksgiving.

Ten months after the Olympic bronze medalist—whose pommel horse performance in the 2024 games earned him the admiration of a nation—and Tess McCraken ended their 10-year relationship, Stephen has hard launched a new romance.

The 28-year-old’s Thanksgiving Day Instagram Story featured a repost from a woman named Annalise, who had shared a photobooth picture strip featuring Stephen. The pair looked very cozy in the snaps, with Stephen even planting a kiss on Annalise’s cheek in the strip’s second photo.

The Olympian has otherwise remained mum on his new relationship, though he follows Annalise on Instagram and commented a fire emoji alongside the word “WOAH” on her Nov. 17 grid post.

Stephen’s new romance comes after he and his former partner Tess, also a gymnast, decided to go their separate ways in January after first finding love at Penn State ten years earlier.

“Stephen and I are no longer together,” Tess revealed in an April 4 TikTok, “and we haven’t been since the beginning of January.”

She shared that while she’d been “putting off” a formal announcement of her and Stephen’s breakup, fans’ sleuthing abilities had forced her hand.

“[My] social media has been cleaned out,” she explained. “I can’t post anything now without getting at least a few comments and I know there have been multiple Reddit threads. And so, I feel like it’s just easier to have it out in the open and not really have to hide it anymore.”

As for what led to her and Stephen parting ways after a decade together, Tess assured fans their breakup had been amicable.

“There was no drama,” she emphasized. “It was really just time, and that sucks a lot. There’s really no other way to put it. We were together for almost 10 years. We met and got together when we were 17 and 18, and we’re now 27 and 28.”

“As it turns out,” she added, “there are things that didn’t matter at 18 that matter when you’re in your later 20s.”

And despite the breakup, Tess—who was by Stephen’s side for the 2024 Games in Paris and his Dancing With the Stars run that same year—confirmed she’ll always be one of his biggest fans.

“There’s no bad blood,” she added. “I want to see him succeed in everything, but the way that support is coming has to be different now.”

As for Stephen, while fans will need to wait to learn more about his winning romance with Annalise, he isn’t the only celebrity who has used social media to hard launch new love. Read on for more.

The supermodel hard launched her romance with the cowboy in November 2026, sharing photos of the two all cozied up at Colorado Avalanche hockey game.

The One Direction singer and the the Love Island alum took the major milestone in their relationship in August 2025, nearly six months after they first sparked romance rumors. McDermott shared the sweet PDA-filled selfie to her page alongside a heart emoji, while Tomlinson commented, "I love you x."

Two years after the supermodel sparked dating rumors with the A Star Is Born actor, the pair went Instagram official with a photo of themselves kissing at Hadid's 30th birthday party.

"I feel so lucky to be 30!" Hadid captioned the Instagram post. "I feel so lucky for every high and low- for all the lessons and gifts both have brought me. To get to feel it all! I’m so lucky to be a mom, friend, partner, sister, daughter, colleague to some of the most unbelievable humans!!"

The "Barbie World" rapper gave fans a taste of her and the NFL player's relationship in a mirror selfie included in a April 2026 photo dump.

The Emily in Paris actor was popping the champère when he hard-launched his romance with the Big Little Lies star in May 2025, posting a photo of them smiling for the camera with Sofi Tukker member Sophie Hawley-Weld during a visit to Slab City, Calif.

However, their relationship didn't last long, with news of their breakup coming out that September.

Two months after the Magic Mike star and the model were seen at an Oscars 2025 after-party, she made their relationship Instagram official

“Happy life to the handsomest, kindest, funniest, stoopidest most gorgeous human ever,” she captioned PDA-packed pics posted on Instagram Stories April 2025. “Merci for making life more beautiful.”

The Riverside alum and the "Rack City" rapper went Instagram official in an April 2025 photo dump.

The duo first sparked romance rumors that February when they sat courtside at the Los Angeles Lakers vs. Charlotte Hornets basketball game. Later that month, they also attended Vanity Fair’s Instagram Young Hollywood party together.

In true Lady Whistledown fashion, the Bridgerton star confirmed romance rumors between her and the Get Even actor—who she was first linked to in 2024—in a February 2025 Instagram post.

One month after he was legally separated from ex-wife Britney Spears, the Traitors alum made his relationship with the real estate agent official, sharing a sweet series of photos to ring in 2025.

The Vanderpump Rules alum went Instagram official with the Sleeping with Sirens musician with a sweet birthday tribute in December 2025, sharing a snap of her looking into his eyes.

Martin reposted the photo, writing “Our Casa Vega Xmas Card.”

Despite keeping his identity hidden before the celebratory Instagram story, Maloney previously shared with fans that she was in love.

“I have a boyfriend,” she revealed in an October episode of her costar Dana Kathan’s podcast Disrespectfully. “He just makes me feel really special, and he’s really special.”

The Magic Mike actor made his relationship with the Winning Time actress Instagram official in February 2024, sharing a photo of her standing in front of flowers and a heart-shaped box of candy.

The hard launch came seven months after Manganiello and Sofia Vergara announced their divorce after seven years married.

The "Graveyard" singer and the Victorious alum spooked fans with a Halloween post in 2023, confirming rumors of their romance. In the photo carousel, Halsey was seen holding Jogia's hand while her back was turned away from the camera.

The two were first spotted kissing on a date one month earlier in Hollywood, and now, the two are engaged. She confirmed as much in September 2024 by responding to a post on X that read, “Halsey says she hopes to marry boyfriend Avan Jogia.”

As for her edits, she simply wrote, “***fiancé Avan Jogia.”

Hard launching on Instagram, the Whine Down podcaster shared a photo of her laughing with the soccer star as he wrapped his arms around her. She captioned the January 2023 post, “Back where is all started.”

More than a year later, the duo—who share son Roman Russell—tied the knot in a July 2024 ceremony in Scotland, though she later revealed they had legally married earlier that year in January.

“Just to have that little something for us,” Kramer—mom to Jolie Caussin and Jace Caussin with ex Mike Caussin—explained in a March 2025 episode of her podcast, “that was special to us, that we didn't announce to everybody.”

The ”We Don’t Talk Anymore” singer announced in October 2022 he was dating someone on The Howard Stern Show, revealing he was “definitely” in love. However, it was not until one month later in December when he shared who that special someone was in an Instagram post.

Puth posted a picture with the College of Charleston alum for his 31st birthday. “Ohhhhh I’m NOT a loser… ‘cause I didn’t lose her!!!”, he wrote under the pictures of the duo kissing in a photobooth. “(Happy birthday to me.)”

#721. McInnes tempers 'anxiety' as Rangers seek top spot

Ryan Naderi has netted some crucial goals for Derek McInnes this term

Derek McInnes says Rangers should not experience any anxiety about the prospect of going top of the Scottish Premiership as the Ibrox side look to extend their four-match winning run.

Rangers host in-form Falkirk on Saturday (15:00 GMT), who have won six on the bounce in the league, and victory would move McInnes' team top before leaders Celtic travel to face Hearts on Sunday.

"I don't think there should be anxiety when you're trying to go top of the league at all," McInnes said.

"Obviously, you want to be top of the league come the end of the season.

"If you've got an opportunity to go there, it's important you try and take it."

Ryan Naderi netted an early second-half equaliser then set up Djeidi Gassama as Rangers turned a 1-0 deficit into a 3-1 lead before Aberdeen scored a consolation in Tuesday's Premiership match at Ibrox.

It was Naderi's 11th goal of the season and McInnes spoke of his awareness of the now Czech Republic international last season while managing Hearts, who have used a data analytics firm for much of their recent recruitment.

"Last January, obviously, when we first saw that Rangers were linked with Naderi, like everything else, I would say to [Hearts sporting director] Graeme Jones, 'how do they rate him?'

"Because you're always curious, it's just the way it is. It's brilliant when you see other teams round about you signing a player that's not rated!

"He was someone that I think was well known to them. Brugge had an interest in Ryan, I think, and I think USG potentially had an interest in him as well but the kind of money, the fee, it just went away from them.

"The feeling was that he could help Rangers and make them better.

"I had a good conversation with Ryan when I first came in the door and what we felt this season could look like for him.

"He's stood up brilliantly to the injuries to Youssef [Chermiti] and Lawrence [Shankland] and he's had to be the guy. He's led the line brilliantly and I love the goals he scores. All top strikers have intelligence to be in the right place at the right time."

Rangers 'dug it out' despite naivety & complacency - McInnes

Visit our Rangers page for all the latest news, analysis and fan views

And the manager reiterated his stance about keeping hold of assets like Naderi through January.

"These conversations that I have with Jim [Gillespie, chief executive] on a regular basis about players that we should be speaking to and trying to address and secure and give them a wee bit more security and a wee bit more comfort for us, these conversations, I think, have been ongoing," McInnes said.

"The club's well aware of what needs to be done and what we shouldn't be doing and Ryan's been part of that conversation."

McInnes' side won 2-1 away to Falkirk in September but the Bairns held Danny Rohl's Rangers to a 0-0 draw at Ibrox last season.

"What they have got is a bit more physicality," McInnes said of the Bairns.

"They can play when they want to play so they've mixed it up a bit this season, I think, and been a wee bit more pragmatic maybe at times as well, but they've still had those results that's got them where they are in the league and we've got a difficult game ahead of ourselves."

#719. Iordanescu ready for Watford 'challenge'

Edward Iordandescu is the first Romanian to manage in the top four tiers of English football

New Watford boss Edward Iordanescu says he has inherited a "challenge" but also "an opportunity" as the club seeks to pull away from the Championship relegation zone.

The 48-year-old has replaced Alessio Dionisi, who was sacked on Sunday after only five months in charge, following a run of seven defeats in 10 league games.

Iordanescu became Watford's sixth new boss in less than 18 months and is the 25th manager since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.

He will take charge of the Hornets for the first time on Saturday when they travel to bottom club Derby County.

The Romanian met the media for the first time on Friday, and set out his vision for his tenure.

The Watford job is Iordanescu's first since leaving Legia Warsaw in October 2025, having won the Polish Super Cup with them last season.

It is the 10th managerial post of his 15-year coaching career, which has taken in Bulgarian club CSKA Sofia as well as Steaua Bucharest and Cluj - who he guided to the Romanian title and two domestic cups after joining midway through the 2020-21 season.

He also spent two and a half years in charge of Romania, guiding them to the last 16 of Euro 2024, where they were beaten by the Netherlands.

However, in his first job in English football, he inherits a Watford side three points above the drop zone and facing a fight for their second-tier status.

"I'm proud more than anything else and I'm honoured and happy to be here, but I'm also very aware of the challenge in front of me," Iordanescu told BBC Three Counties Radio.

"I don't want to make promises. I know the fans are not happy in this moment, but also I know that my words are not enough to bring them back, so they wait for facts. We need that, but of course there is a lot of work to do, there is a process in front of us and I hope we make the next steps right away.

"For me it's a challenge but at the same time it's an opportunity and I want to transform this opportunity into something good for the club, for the fans. This is the most important [thing]."

Prior to the dismissal of Dionisi, former Watford player Tom Ince - who left the club at the end of the 2025-26 season - told the BBC's 72+ Podcast there was "so much control away from the manager" at Vicarage Road.

While Ince, now at League Two side Tranmere Rovers, added his respect of positives of chairman Gino Pozzo's practises, he is not alone in speaking out about the board's influence.

Former England boss Sam Allardyce stated he turned down the Watford job in 2019 after claiming he was told how the side should play and which players should be in the XI.

But Iordandescu revealed that is not his expectation.

"I know my borders and I know my responsibilities." he said. "I'm in this club with a lot of quality people, professionals, people that know, understand, in detail, football, but starting yesterday I'm the number one in the technical side.

"I don't believe there's somebody here in the club that can overcome the coach, taking the technical knowledge, so it will be my responsibility, but also the technical part will be my decision all the time."

Pioneer or coach-eater? The complex world of Pozzo's Watford

From a purely statistical perspective, Watford's laboured start to the season under Dionisi could be credited to one key deficiency.

The Hornets have scored the fewest goals in the Championship, with only 13 in their 17 matches so far.

However, Iordanescu said his primary objective was not to thrill, but to win.

He said: "I always prefer to win 1-0 than 4-2. One-nil means you have an organised team, a team with some responsibility to engage 100% and to give everything for the result.

"So for me the priority is not to score more goals - [it is] to start to be organised, to start to act and react together on the pitch, to start to understand that the mindset should be a little bit different than what it was until now and to start to be efficient.

"In time we will see about scoring more goals, definitely every coach wants the team to score as much as possible."

Iordanescu also appeared to confirm he was in talks about taking over while Dionisi was still in charge.

It was reported on 12 November that the Hertfordshire club were in talks with him, but Dionisi, who had only been appointed in June, remained in charge across the international break and for Saturday's 4-0 defeat at Sheffield United.

The Italian was sacked on Sunday, with Iordanescu appointed on Wednesday.

Iordanescu said he had "asked for time" from the Watford hierachy before accepting the role.

He said: "I wanted to understand very clearly the objectives, the targets, so when I gave the final response, I was aware of everything.

"I'm here, I'm enthusiastic, I'm positive, I'm confident we can do good things together, and the thing which I count most on is the potential of this very young team. One of the youngest teams in the league."

But Iordanescu also took time to pay tribute to his predecessor.

"He [Dionisi] definitely worked hard," said Iordanescu.

"He did and left good things, very good things, already I saw many of them. But in football when things don't run the way you want and when the results are not backing up your work, it's difficult.

"I know he is a coach that put a lot of heart in his work and thank him for the good things that he did, and also tried to achieve here."

The task at hand now for Iordanescu is to succeed where Dionisi, and so many other Hornets bosses since their Premier League relegation in 2022, could not.

#718. EU and Indonesia sign trade deal

A deal covering 730 million people promises lower tariffs and new investment opportunities as the European Union seeks to diversify trade ties amid growing global economic tensions.

The European Union and Indonesia signed a free trade deal on Saturday, describing it as a new chapter in economic relations between the two sides.

"This is one of the most ambitious deals the European Union has concluded in Asia," Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, said at the signing ceremony on Saturday.

"Together, we represent a market of 730 million people," she added.

The Indonesia-European Union Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) and the additional Investment Protection Agreement (IPA) are designed to reduce trade barriers and attract investment in strategic sectors such as electric vehicles, electronics, and pharmaceuticals.

The agreement comes after almost 10 years of negotiations and is part of a wider series of trade deals by the EU.

The bloc hopes to reduce its reliance on individual economic partners as trade with both China and the US has become more difficult in recent years.

Von der Leyen also stressed the importance of international cooperation, saying that "in a time when others are closing their doors, we keep ours open."

The deal sees tariffs on about 98% of EU exports to Indonesia to be done away with. The EU estimates that European companies could save more than €600 million (around $658 million) per year.

"The benefits for our exporters are concrete and measurable," Indonesian Minister of Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto said, hailing a "new chapter" in economic relations with the EU. He said the deal would benefit his country’s main exports to Europe, including palm oil, footwear and textiles.

Palm oil and deforestation had been major stumbling blocks during the negotiations, and the agreement includes mechanisms for cooperation on regulatory and sustainability issues as well as a dedicated protocol on palm oil to address environmental concerns.

The EU parliament is now expected to greenlight the deal while Indonesian authorities will also complete the ratification process so it can enter into force in 2027.

#717. Bournemouth 'allowed to dream' as fans book Europa League final hotels

Marco Rose replaced Andoni Iraola - who ended up at Liverpool - in the summer

Bournemouth are dreaming of winning the Europa League after staging a 10-man fightback to join a select band of teams to win their first five European games.

The Cherries trailed 1-0 to Iago Aspas' goal at Celta Vigo, and then went down to 10 men midway through the first half when Bafode Diakite was sent off.

But second-half goals from Alvaro Rodriguez and Rayan gave the Cherries a 10th consecutive win in all competitions, extending their club record run.

Bournemouth are only the third side to win each of their first five European matches (excluding qualifiers and including the Inter-Cities Fairs Cup), after Nuremberg in 1961-62 and Ararat in 1972-73.

They top this season's table as the only club to win five out of five - and are closing in on a top-eight spot, which would mean they skip a play-off round and go straight into the last 16.

Some fans have told the BBC they have already booked hotels in Frankfurt for the final on 26 May.

As supporters sang about reaching that game, midfielder Alex Scott was asked for his thoughts on TNT Sports.

"Of course that's our dream. When you grow up wanting to be a footballer you dream of winning trophies," Scott said.

"Where this club has come from to where it is now, full credit to everyone who has built it.

"For players, it's a dream to be on the pitch playing for this club. We have still got wins to get to qualify into the top eight, and from there all focus is on pushing forward and hopefully we can go on and win it."

'Living the dream' - Bournemouth fan after Europa League win

The Cherries are in unprecedented times, with their biggest trophy to date being when they won the second-tier Championship in 2014-15.

In terms of cups, they won the 1983â84 Associate Members' Cup - which later became the EFL Trophy.

Head coach Marco Rose, who replaced Andoni Iraola in the summer, said: "It's always allowed to dream.

"If you get a competition like this you want to achieve the best possible thing. We know it's far away to go. Many games. Now it's about getting into the top eight to avoid more games and then we can see step by step."

As well as just winning their games, Bournemouth are firing in the goals. They have netted at least twice in each match during this 10-game winning run.

And they are the first side to score at least twice in each of their first five matches in Europe since Queens Park Rangers in 1976.

The win on Thursday was made even more impressive by the fact they contested 75% of the game with 10 men.

It came days after Manchester United seemed to implode after an early red card against Liverpool, losing 4-0.

Former England manager Glenn Hoddle said on TNT: "They have deserved this result. They've played beautifully with 10 men - probably as good as I've seen a team play defensively and with the ball.

"I've not seen a team go down to 10 men for so long and dictate a game and deserve to win the game. They were absolutely brilliant."

Cherries boss Rose told BBC Radio Solent: "What a team, what a spirit, what an energy.

"I said to Ty [Tyler Adams] sometimes it's not about tactics and formations and stuff like this. [David] Brooks did a great job when we got one player less - he played right defender like he played it for 10 years. We changed in the right moment. Everyone did his job on a really high level.

"We were just relentless and we never stopped to believe in this win and that's why big, big, big congratulations to the team.

"You feel if you're one player down that it's a difficult night, but to handle a difficult night like this, it just shows the character of the team and of the whole group."

The coach's belief in what they are doing filters through to the players.

Amine Adli, who set up the equaliser, told the BBC: "At half-time, everyone still believed we can turn the game in our way and this is what happened.

"Everyone was like 'guys we can make it, we have to believe. If we score the game can change.'"

Earlier this month, the attacking midfielder said he saw a lot of similarities to the Bayer Leverkusen team he was part of in 2023-24.

That is not a bad comparison, considering they went unbeaten to win the domestic double, as well as reaching the Europa League final.

So who can blame the Cherries for dreaming?

#716. 'Priceless' Duran proves 'the man' but is he papering over cracks at Celtic?

Camilo Duran's 15-goal haul this season has made him an invaluable player for a Celtic side fighting for European progression

"Duran is priceless for us at the moment".

It would be difficult for a football manager to muster up a higher compliment for one of his players - given he should know exactly how much he did cost - but Celtic boss Martin O'Neill was rightly effusive in his praise for Camilo Duran.

With 15 goals in 23 appearances, six assists, and another late European winner on Thursday, the Colombian was once again the main man for a struggling Celtic side.

His double against Besiktas breathed life into their Europa League campaign last time out, and his late leap to nod in the winner against Torreense kept it alive.

Duran, 24, started on the bench but was brought on with just over half an hour to go as O'Neill watched his side labour against a team currently 13th in the Portuguese second tier.

Celtic would still be searching for their first European win were it not for their summer arrival from Qarabag, whose goals have played a key part in keeping his team within touching distance of a play-off spot with three fixtures to play.

"He's taken on this mantle of being the man and he's been fantastic," said O'Neill, who started Duran on the bench. "We tried a similar approach against Besiktas.

"Sometimes by the time Duran gets subbed on, you could be behind. But I think that's the sign of a brilliant player, he'll do something.

"He's not a big guy but he's just a super footballer, a super, super footballer."

'He's priceless for us' - O'Neill on match winner Duran

Duran's summer arrival was overshadowed when, just over a fortnight later, a club-record fee was paid to Bodo Glimt for another striker, Kasper Hogh.

While recent weeks have been dominated by debates over Duran or Hogh, the debate now seems settled, with the Colombian operating on a different level from his striking counterpart.

Anyone watching Celtic in Portugal would have watched Hogh find space a handful of times in the area, but repeatedly fail to find a team-mate or trouble the goalkeeper. Duran didn't need to be asked twice.

"I don't know how many touches he got, but he had the telling touch," James McFadden said on Sportsound post-match.

Duran's goals have also proved decisive in securing domestic points against Falkirk and Hibernian, and with Celtic just a point clear of Rangers, he is indeed invaluable.

Despite his late header giving the thousands of travelling Celtic fans a thrilling end to a relatively turgid game, the intervention is another significant moment in a season that is threatening to unravel if individual performances fail to continue papering over glaring deficiencies across the park.

If the lively Jota - who lasted 74 minutes - was not creating chances, tormenting full-backs or digging out enticing crosses in the first half, Celtic seemed without any real plan of attack.

Yang and Luke McCowan's involvements were limited at best, Hogh's chance to stake a claim was sub-par to be kind, and there was no driving force from the middle of the park to show some impetus.

Arithmetically, Celtic can still finish in any position in the Europa League table. But if they are to claim a playoff or automatic qualification spot, they will need Duran to remain in such a rich vein of form.

Duran spares Celtic's blushes against Portuguese second-tier side Torreense

Brian: Embarrassed by that performance, I know that there no easy games in Europe, couldn't pass the ball, not fit enough, no style of play and poorly coached. The club is in decline.

John: Celtic are just an average side these days - there should be no expectation.

Ted: That was just embarrassing. The 31st team in Portugal made us look ordinary. Go now Martin with dignity intact and preserve your achievements. Thus mob will drag you down.

Allan: Outclassed and out paced by Torreense, Celtic played poorly with a lot of comedy of errors in their play. But Yippee hee, Celtic. Won with a late goal from Duran.

Liam: This can't go on any further now, regardless of the result. MON is done and the coaching staff are done. Booing substitutions is the end, never mind a performance like this against second division opposition. The board can resign too.

Alec: Total embarrassment. Barring Jota, there was a complete lack of creativity, quality, urgency and belief. Time for the board to make the right decisions, get a new manager in and get rid of at least 10 of those players on show tonight.
