#684. COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use

After two weeks of tough talks, the COP31 climate summit has closed without a consensus on how to quit fossil fuels or fund countries struggling to adapt to a hotter world.

Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.

After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU said it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.

"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time," said Irish climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU on Sunday.

He said adopting a decision that omitted fossil fuels would be "unconscionable" and risked "deepening the chasm between global commitment and the action required."

Panama also rejected the deal, describing it as a step backwards in addressing the climate crisis, and adding that any decision must acknowledge "the truth about the collective failure on 1.5 degrees Celsius [2.7 degrees Fahrenheit]." That is the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avert runaway climate change.

"Those who contributed to this crisis ... must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it," the Panamanian delegation said.

The Marshall Islands, which faces an existential threat from sea level rise, formally objected to the cover decision, saying "we will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests."   Chris ⁠Bowen, Australia's COP31 negotiating president ‌⁠said the breakdown in talks was very ‌disappointing. Russia, however, supported the decision to leave out wording on accelerating a phaseout of fossil fuels, arguing that they are still a necessary power source and that each country should be able to determine its own pathway on how to cut emissions.

Pakistan and Ghana, defended the agreement as a necessary compromise in the spirit of multilateralism. "We need to build bridges not barriers," said the Pakistan negotiator.

The marathon talks, held at a time when the window is rapidly closing to avoid the escalating impacts of climate change, including drought, deadly heat and flooding, also saw major disputes over financing.   Developing states blamed the collapse in talks on the EU and other wealthier nations for failing to scale up financing to help them adapt to climate-linked weather extremes and the damage they cause. The EU is the largest provider of climate finance and has resisted new adaptation finance targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign accused wealthy countries of demanding greater climate ambition while refusing to stump up the cash to pay for it.

"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he added.

The final cover decision had proposed further discussions on "an implementation pathway for tripling adaptation finance by 2035" but without mentioning a figure. It noted that developing countries need some $300 billion annually for adaptation until 2035, and expressed concern about "the gap between climate finance flows and needs."

Outside formal negotiations, a separate initiative to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) has been gaining momentum.

Maina Talia, Tuvalu's minister for climate change and the environment, said TAFF was "moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed plans for a global transformation."

At the same time, a growing number of states, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany and Finland, have either completed or are working on so-called national roadmaps to wean themselves off fossil fuels. But Brandon Wu, director of Policy and Campaigns ActionAid USA, dismissed such plans as "meaningless" and "nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy" on the part of rich countries not stepping up on climate finance. "COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it's because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise. They may as well have come to the COP shouting at vulnerable communities: 'we don't care if you die.'"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The rejected cover decision had recognized that electrification can deliver emissions reductions, improve energy security and expand access to energy.

It included a call to increase the share of electricity in final energy demand from around 20% now to 35% by 2035 — a proposal heavily touted by co-host Turkey. Still, about 75 countries, including solar powerhouse China, adopted the pledge outside of the formal negotiations. It is non-binding and does not specify whether that additional electricity must come from clean sources. Critics say this leaves open the possibility that expanded electricity demand could be met by fossil fuels.

The talks in Turkey marked the first time a COP was taking place under the explicit knowledge that global temperatures will exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Countries were split on how to deal with that so-called "overshoot."

The cover decision had called on states to commit to limiting overshoot , acknowledging that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.”

It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" emissions cuts and for action on ramping down potent greenhouse gas methane.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Another contenious issue at the talks and in the final draft decision was a call for "increasing" carbon capture and storage technologies that entails capturing CO2 and burying it. The text said the world should aim to reach "gigaton scale" by 2035.

Scientists say some carbon removal technologies will be necessary to curb emissions and bring temperatures back down. But critics argue they are unproven at scale, expensive and risk giving polluters an excuse to keep burning fossil fuels.

Vanuatu's climate minister Ralph Regenvanu said carbon capture and storage "had been singled out for special attention that it doesn't deserve."

The stakes were high at COP31. The summit followed a string of recent climate-related disasters, from deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.

At the same time, geopolitical shocks that sent oil prices rising globally shifted the focus onto energy security and the future of fossil fuels.

Speaking near the end of the conference in Antalya, Ethiopian foreign minister Gedion Timothewos, who will preside over COP32, said his country aimed to "restore hope, rebuild trust and mobilize collective action" at the next summit to be held in 2027 in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa.

"We will work with you all to rebuild confidence in multilateral climate cooperation. This confidence must be earned through delivery. The decisions we take at COPs must advance climate action and implementation."

With reporting from Tim Schauenberg and Katharina Schantz in Antalya.

#683. Candace Cameron Bure Says She Gets “Substantial” Residuals From ‘Full House’

The actress played D.J. Tanner throughout the show's run from 1987 to 1995, and later reprised her role in the sitcom’s spin-off 'Fuller House.'

Candace Cameron Bure is getting candid about the residuals she still earns from Full House.

The actress appeared on a recent episode of The McBride Rewind podcast, where she revealed that she gets “substantial” payouts from the sitcom, which ran for eight seasons from 1987 to 1995.

“They’re substantial… I think it’s like quarterly,” she said, noting that while some residual checks for other projects might be a few cents or dollars, the ones for Full House are “still substantial.” Related Stories Lifestyle Dave Coulier Says Cancer Treatment Has Led to Changes in His Speech and Physical Appearance Movies Why Candace Cameron Bure Says Horror Films Can Lead to a "Portal" That's "Incredibly Demonic"

“I’m always happy when I open that check and deposit it,” Bure added.

The actress played D.J. Tanner, the eldest sister to Stephanie (Jodie Sweetin) and Michelle (Mary-Kate/Ashley Olsen), throughout the show’s run. She also reprised her role in the sitcom’s spin-off Fuller House, which ran for five seasons from 2016 to 2020.

Host Josh McBride also brought up Sweetin’s appearance on the podcast in April 2026, where she shared that her residuals aren’t as great as they used to be.

“I got a one-cent check the other day. No, there’s no syndication anymore because it’s all in streaming. Who gets paid for that? Nobody gets paid for that,” Sweetin said at the time. “Sure, in my 20s, there would be money, but not reliable. You don’t know how much it’s going to be or how often they’re going to run the show. So, sometimes you’re like, ‘Oh, cool. That was nice.’ And then sometimes you’re like, ‘All right, well, there’s a nice dinner out.'”

In response, Bure told McBride, “I actually saw that and she said she doesn’t get much now. And I was like, ‘Jodie, you gotta check with your agent or you gotta call your bank,’ ’cause I still get residuals.”

Elsewhere on the podcast, Bure also addressed the Olsen twins’ decision not to appear on the spin-off. “It was a bummer because it would have been fun to have everybody back,” she said of Fuller House. “But at the same time, it wasn’t surprising just because none of us really have stayed close with the girls.”

“Not because anything went wrong or there was any bad blood. I just think they were kids. They were [filming from] 9 months old until they were 8 years old. They have very different memories than we do. Even me being 10 years older than them, I have significant, great, wonderful memories,” she continued. “They were babies. They probably don’t even remember half the stuff [we do]. They didn’t have the attachment to the crew and the people like we did being older. And they had such a successful fashion business. They haven’t been actors for a long time. They just haven’t been in that part of entertainment.”

With the Roots backing them up, Fallon opened the show with Timberlake for a song and dance number, with the duo going through The History of Party Songs. In a segment that is catnip for 90s kids, the tracks covered included Soul II Soul’s “Back to Life (However Do You Want Me),” Ini Kamoze’s “Here Comes the Hotstepper,” Mark Morrison’s “Return of the Mack,” Montell Jordan’s “This Is How We Do It,” Spice Girls “Wannabe,” Bell Biv DeVoe’s “Poison,” Timberlake’s own “Rock Your Body” and more.

In the interview section, Timberlake opened up about the making of FutureSex/LoveSounds, reminding the audience that that his influences on the album included “Bowie, David Byrne, Talking Heads, Freddie Mercury, Queen, Billy Idol, James Brown, Eurythmics and INXS.” He said that on the song “SexyBack” he was channeling Bowie doing “Rebel Rebel” and he had to fight the recording company on the production. “They fought me on it. Well, I brought it in and it was like, ‘It’s too fast.’ I was like, ‘That’s why it’s gonna work.’ … [And they said], ‘You don’t sound like you, your signature falsetto.’ I was like, ‘That’s why it’s gonna work.'”

On the infamous lyrics to “SexyBack”, Timberlake added, “That song does not make any sense. I’ve said this. It makes zero sense. But, it’s why it makes sense.”

In a particularly poignant part of the interview, Timberlake discussed his love for and influence of the late D’Angelo, describing him as “my guy.” “D’Angelo, for me, he changed everything. You know, he was one of those artists… rest in peace. What a brilliant, brilliant, brilliant artist. But I remember when he came out, it just like everything changed. [He] was a once-in-a-generation artist.”

On why he decided to take part in the Apple docuseries — which Fallon said tackled Timberlake’s career highpoints and personal low points — the Grammy-winner said that initially he “was really reluctant to do it” agreeing with Fallon that he was “sort of famously private.” His relationship with director Fisher Stevens softened his stance and that the doc he has “mustered up some courage to talk about some things that I’ve never talked about before, that, you know, things that even those that are closest to me don’t know.”

Timberlake said he found the doc experience “cathartic” and he hoped it would help others to share their troubles. “Everybody’s going through something. And I think I’ve gone through a lot in the last five years that I feel like have made me a better human and a better father, a better husband, a better friend.”

In the recent past, Timberlake has had a number of public incidents including being arrested for DWI in the Hamptons in June 2024 and revealing in July 2025 that he was diagnosed with Lyme disease. There was also the cheating rumors in 2019, and subsequent public ridicule, after the singer was caught holding hands with co-star Alisha Wainwright during the filming of Palmer. Timberlake had to issue a public apology about the Palmer incident on Instagram, calling it a “strong lapse in judgment.”

One sketch that’s likely to get a lot of play on social media was “Sexy Butterball Hotline,” where Fallon (Rocky Drumstick) and Timberlake (Pecker Spatchcock) played two very sexy turkeys — “the dirtiest birds in the coop” no less — manning an after dark Thanksgiving helpline. A sample of some of the lines from Rocky and Pecker in this bit: “Who says the turkey can’t be the one who does the stuffing?” “Is it Black Friday? ‘Cause my clothes are 100% off.” “I can’t wait till you lay me down on the table right in front of Grandma.” Good clean fun.

It wouldn’t be a complete Timberlake Tonight Show appearance without a “Camp Winnipesaukee” sketch. Fallon and Timberlake once more donned the retainers and wigs to relive their awkward teenage years and play the annoying campers trying to sing a popular song much to the annoyance of the camp counselor. On Thursday’s episode, the pair decided to take on The Proclaimers’ 1988 hit “I’m Gonna Be (500 Miles)” with Timberlake and Fallon’s attempt at Scottish brogue worthy of commendation but ultimately short of passable.

Proving he’s still one of the greatest singers and dancers around, Timberlake rounded his appearance with two medleys of his greatest hits. In the first clip he performed a medley of “FutureSex / LoveSound,” “SexyBack,” “Summer Love” and “My Love.”

In a second clip he performed “LoveStoned,” “Until the End of Time” and “What Goes Around…/ … Comes Around.”

#680. Audible’s Black Friday Deal Gets You a Subscription to Bestselling Books for Only $.99 Per Month

Until Dec. 28, Audible's biggest sale of the season gives eligible customers 90% off a Standard membership, bringing the monthly price down to just $0.99.

All products and services featured are independently chosen by editors. However, Billboard may receive a commission on orders placed through its retail links, and the retailer may receive certain auditable data for accounting purposes.

Sometimes the best holiday shopping purchases are something for yourself, especially if it means having a new stack of audiobooks ready for the holidays.

I recently took advantage of the deal during my travels from Los Angeles to Edinburgh this week. I listened to Straight from the Heart, Bonnie Tyler’s memoir, narrated by the singer herself. It’s an intimate yet often funny account of her life, including how using her voice too soon after vocal cord surgery contributed to her signature raspy tone. I downloaded it before travelling so I could listen offline on the plane and also saved Dolly Parton’s Star of the Show: My Life on Stage to listen to later on.

With Audible Standard, you can choose one audiobook each month to keep in your library, revisit whenever you like and purchase additional titles separately if you whizz through them like me.

Brandy’s memoir was a major hit when it came out, becoming a New York Times bestseller a month after its release. It’s a must-read for fans who’ve followed her career since the ’90s. From Moesha and her iconic Cinderella role alongside Whitney Houston to her chart-topping hits, there’s plenty of nostalgia in this book. Brandy is also set to reunite with Monica for their 10-show The Boy Is Mine Las Vegas residency in 2027, making this a particularly good time to revisit her story.

With the next instalment of Cher’s memoir coming in November 2027, now is the perfect opportunity to catch up on the first chapter of the Grammy winner’s story. Cher: Part One explores her childhood, extraordinary rise to fame and turbulent marriage to Sonny Bono. Among its most striking revelations are allegations of financial control, infidelity and Bono’s admission that he had contemplated killing her. There’s plenty to discover before the next volume picks up around 1980.

As a huge Liza Minnelli fan, this is high on my listening list. Narrated by the EGOT-winning entertainer herself, the memoir promises an unfiltered look at growing up as the daughter of Judy Garland and Vincente Minnelli. Liza explores fame, relationships, addiction, health struggles and her remarkable career.

Published just three years before her sudden death in 2026, Bonnie Tyler’s memoir feels especially poignant now. Narrated by the Welsh singer herself, Straight from the Heart is a chance to hear her tell her own story, from the highs of international stardom to the personal experiences behind that unmistakable raspy voice. It’s candid, funny and a lovely tribute to a music legend.

Published in 2025, Dolly Parton’s photo memoir includes a downloadable companion PDF featuring a selection of photographs from the hardcover edition. The book follows Parton’s remarkable seven decades as a live performer, taking fans behind the scenes of her legendary career on stage. Co-written and co-narrated by Parton and Tom Roland, the audiobook is a particularly special listen for Dolly fans, offering a chance to hear the country music icon reflect on her extraordinary life and legacy so soon after her death.

Former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick revisits the protest that changed his career and made him one of the most talked-about athletes in America. After taking a knee during the national anthem in 2016, he became a polarising figure and ultimately never returned to the NFL. This memoir offers his perspective on the controversy and the personal experiences behind his decision.

An instant No. 1 New York Times bestseller, Famesick is the latest from Lena Dunham, the creator and star of HBO’s Girls. Known for turning her personal life into compelling on-screen storytelling, Dunham takes a similarly candid approach here, reflecting on fame, relationships and the health struggles that have shaped her life behind the scenes. Expect plenty of honesty and her signature self-deprecating humour.

I love a good audiobook, but I also adore the feel and smell of a physical book in my hands. That’s why I make a point of enjoying both formats throughout the year at a 50/50 ratio. My annual goal is to read 15 physical books and listen to 15 audiobooks, a balance that has worked well for me for years.

As an avid audiobook listener, one of my favourite Audible features is the adjustable narration speed. I usually start at normal speed to get familiar with the narrator before cranking it up to double speed once I’m settled in. The ability to download audiobooks, podcasts and Originals is another benefit, especially when travelling and without Wi-Fi on a plane. I also love the sleep timer, chapter navigation and the ability to sync my listening progress across devices. Moreover, the Audible Read & Listen feature allows you to pair eligible audiobooks with Kindle editions to follow along as you read.

#679. Arthur Conti Was Booked This Year With Roles in ‘Carrie’ and ‘Ebenezer.’ Now He’s Looking to Get “a Little Strange”

The 22-year-old has tackled iconic characters in pop culture this year, but he's keeping himself open about what's next.

British actor Arthur Conti is fresh off a whirlwind year. With roles in Mike Flanagan’s Carrie adaptation and the recently released Ebenezer, he’s been busy crafting new interpretations of well-known characters.

“To play an iconic character that’s been played by many people before, and to get to give your own spin on it, is very exciting,” Conti tells The Hollywood Reporter over Zoom from London about what he’s been up to this year.

The 22-year-old actor is back in the U.K. after over a month of press for Carrie and Ebenezer and a stint in Portland, Oregon. “It’s been a bit of a whirlwind, but it’s been very enjoyable,” he says. After a breakout performance in 2024’s Beetlejuice Beetlejuice, 2026 has been the actor’s biggest year to date between the two projects and a role in Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Related Stories TV Why Mike Flanagan Just Couldn't Kill Carrie White Movies 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Slays $120M at Box Office as Franchise Heats Back Up

With Carrie, Conti stepped into the role of teen bully Billy Nolan, first played on screen by John Travolta in Brian De Palma’s 1976 film. Conti had read Stephen King’s novel but hadn’t seen De Palma’s film, which he stayed away from during filming. Conti’s Billy, while still one of the villains of the story, is different from Travolta’s take on the character. “I was worried that even inadvertently or subconsciously I would copy things about that performance, and I really wanted it to be all my own,” he says.

Ebenezer finds Conti stepping into the shoes of the titular character of Ebenezer Scrooge — well, the younger version of him anyway. The actor heard that Ti West would be making the film, and as a big fan, he sent in a self-tape. Much like with Carrie, he tried not to take too much inspiration from previous versions of the story, but there’s one adaptation that stands out.

“[The Muppets version] is probably the best one. I mean, it’s amazing, that film. Michael Caine gives such a genuinely brilliant, dramatic performance in that film against the Muppets,” he says. “He takes it so seriously, and that is the beauty of that film is that you’d think he was talking to John Gielgud, and he’s talking to Fozzy.”

Despite The Muppets Christmas Carol being his main experience with the story beforehand, he did watch the 1951 film adaptation starring Alastair Sim as Scrooge. “I really liked,” he notes.

Below, the actor digs into his last year in roles, what he’s looking to do next and how he’d spend a perfect day in London.

I’m always curious, as someone who enjoys it — have you seen Carrie: The Musical?

We watched it. We saw a theater production on Granville Island in Vancouver. It was a youth theater production of Carrie: The Musical. [The cast of Carrie] all went to go and see it. Mike [Flanagan] actually put the cast of that production of Carrie in the show. They’re all at the prom. Throughout the show, they’re in the background at the school, which was really, really fun.

How has the year been? You were busy with Carrie and now Ebenezer.

[Carrie] was my first big press tour. It was my first time doing a press junket and all of these things. It feels like the biggest thing that I’ve done so far [with] how much I’ve been promoting it. It was all incredibly exciting. [In Carrie,] I’m playing another character that has several sides to him, after [I did in] Beetlejuice. It’s another deceptively charming, manipulative character, which is interesting that I keep taking. (Laughs).

Something about me, I don’t know. Something untrustworthy. Honestly, it is a treat to play characters like that because you get the chance to do multiple things at once, present a character that has many layers and is complex and isn’t wholly one thing or another. It was a great role. It was a really meaty role to sink my teeth into, and it was an honor to play a character of that literary significance. It was a privilege to be entrusted with that.

As an actor, are you drawn to characters that are different from you, then?

It’s nice to get outside of yourself — that’s part of the fun of it. Growing up, the films I was watching, I was a lot more drawn to flawed or strange or darker characters. I grew up watching Steve Buchemi in Fargo and Philip Seymour Hoffman in Punch-Drunk Love and Talented Mr. Ripley. Those are the kind of characters that I always really loved to watch.

The scope of the projects you had this year has been quite large. Are you drawn to that or looking to change it?

You’re right. They are quite large-scale. I think I’m drawn to things that are a little out there and a little strange. Horror is one of the best genres to explore that area because it emboldens filmmakers to experiment and take risks and be a bit weird and a bit dreamlike. That’s why I gravitate towards horror a lot, and it’s probably what I watch the most of in the cinema.

Is that where you got your love for it? Were you big into horror as a kid?

I think so. It’s not horror, just things that are a little strange. My mom brought me up on Charlie Kaufman films. Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind is my mom’s favorite film, so I watched that quite early. Things that tap into that dreaminess and that weirdness and spookiness — that’s up my alley. But it would be a dream to do a Before Sunrise kind of thing, where it’s just two people talking for an hour and a half. I would love to do something like that next.

Is that what you’re looking to do going forward then?

It could be anything. I really want to leave myself open. I would love to do something a little more scaled down, kind of dialogue-heavy thing. I could never have imagined the caliber of director and the caliber of actor that I’ve been working with. If I can only just continue to do that, I will be very lucky indeed. I’ve gotten to work with some of my absolute heroes, and that’s been wonderful. But I want to keep working in horror as well. Horror’s having a really exciting moment right now, especially young people in horror, with Obsession and Backrooms. I will stay as long as it’ll have me. Horror, fantasy — that’s what I grew up with, and I want to explore that more as well.

I would wake up at 10:30 a.m.-ish. I’m a very late-to-bed, late-to-rise kind of person in my free time. I’d wake up then; I’d get a coffee; I’d go for a walk. I have to do 10,000 steps a day. I’m like a dog. I have to be walked. Then I would go and see a movie. I would go to the cinema. I would probably go to the Prince Charles Cinema, which is my favorite in the world. I don’t know whether I’d see it on my own or with somebody else. I do go on my own to the cinema a lot. That’s one of my favorite ways to watch a film. Then I’d get a nice dinner. I might go shopping a little bit. I might go record shopping, go DVD shopping. Then I would go to the pub maybe, and then I would go to bed at 1 a.m. I’m being very specific with the times.

I’m unfamiliar with Prince Charles Cinema; why is that your favorite theater?

Just the vibe there, and the programming. There’s always something on there that’s worth seeing. I honestly have so much to thank that cinema for because the education in film that it has given me is just insane. I’ve seen so many films there for the first time. It’s one of the few places, in London especially, where you can see old films and cult films and things that don’t get screened very often. You can go and experience them in the theater, and that’s a very valuable thing. They were going to possibly get shut down, but they’ve just won the battle against the landlord or whatever. They’re going to be there for another 25 years. I’m very happy about that.

#676. The Ultimate Thanksgiving Detox? Mexico’s Most Over-the-Top, Celeb-Approved Longevity Clinic

A new wellness resort is attracting a glittery crowd with outré longevity offerings. Rectal ozone therapy, anyone?

Pampering spa getaways are so passé. The reinvented power trip? Longevity-centered five-star resorts that zero in on preventive medicine and rigorous cutting-edge health-optimization treatments. Think Benjamin Button-like cellular reprogramming and biotech breakthroughs that promise to help rewind biological aging in the elite quest to amp up health span.

Once confined largely to Switzerland, top-tier medi-wellness destinations are moving closer to Hollywood. Most notable among them is SHA Mexico, which opened in 2024 on a beachfront stretch of Costa Mujeres, north of Cancún. The flagship avant-garde longevity clinic, SHA Spain, launched in 2008 in the coastal town of L’Albir, has welcomed pro athletes, royalty, supermodels and such stars as Barbra Streisand (for repeat visits), Demi Moore, Monica Bellucci, Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz, Lily James, Madonna and Marisa Tomei. Now names like Dakota Johnson, Kate Moss, Jack Black, Pink, model Candice Swanepoel and Lake Bell are on the guest list at the Mexican outpost. Related Stories Lifestyle The 5 Best Red Light Therapy Panels for Improving Your Health At-Home Lifestyle Jennifer Aniston Joins Boyfriend Jim Curtis For Chat About Health, Wellness and Hypnotherapy

Calling to mind The Jetsons’ Googie-style home in Orbit City, the futuristic design, by Mexican architecture studio Sordo Madaleno, was aptly inspired by the human genome. Exclusive to this location is a bank of stem cells, unveiled in June, ethically sourced from embryonic tissues for medical and aesthetic cellular regeneration therapies that target autoimmune disease, muscle injuries, sleep apnea, aging skin and more. (At SHA Spain, therapies use the patient’s own stem cells; these donor-derived regenerative treatments are not yet approved in the U.S. or Europe for the uses described.) Treatments are administered through intravenous infusions, nebulizer inhalation and targeted injection; exosome facials inject the cell-derived donor particles directly into the face.

“These therapies reprogram the body’s natural mechanisms to heal and rejuvenate from the inside out,” says Dr. Andrea Márquez, head of SHA’s regenerative medicine, explaining that aging or inflamed cellular systems need a reboot.

A Cell Regeneration Therapy bed with a “human regenerator device” is said to boost energy, support physical recovery and promote anti-aging benefits by surrounding the body with a field of electrically charged particles.

A popular European beauty secret, not yet available in the U.S. and offered at SHA Mexico, is Profhilo, the Italian hyaluronic acid-based skin remodeling injectable that improves elasticity.

More than 200 SHA offerings range from neurocognitive, hormonal and sleep health to genomic medicine, dermatology and physiotherapy. Each guest is prescribed teas and an anti-inflammatory vegan or pescatarian diet, with add-ons like seaweed or shots of apple cider vinegar. SHA’s Japanese-influenced dietary rules discourage liquid drinks during meals (said to “hinder digestion”), and breakfast kicks off with a bowl of miso soup (probiotic-rich to support gut health).

One gut-health package popular with the Hollywood crowd promises to detox and optimize the digestive system. Included are an intestinal dysbiosis analysis, visceral osteopathy (hands-on manipulation of the abdomen intended to improve function of internal organs) and intestinal ozone therapy. Not FDA-approved as a medical treatment in the U.S., the latter pumps an oxygen/ozone gas mixture into the rectum to purportedly “reduce oxidative stress, support immune balance and promote tissue repair,” according to the SHA website.

Gwyneth Paltrow and self-proclaimed “father of biohacking” Dave Asprey have both fessed to using rectal ozone therapy. Vaginal ozone therapy and ozone IV infusions (also used by Asprey) are additionally on the service menu, as is a dental cleaning that incorporates the agent.

Hollywood dermatologist Ava Shamban (whose clients include Moore, Angela Bassett, Nicole Kidman and Michelle Yeoh) weighs in on donor stem cells and ozone treatments: “I say proceed with caution. The science is soft. The good news is that we are on the cusp of truly groundbreaking longevity sciences that will come with DNA optimization and literal reversal of aging, using the newest technologies.”

As over-the-top as some of this may seem, SHA’s owners are firmly at the forefront of longevity research: “It’s not just about trendy biohacking and optimization; we have built a legacy approaching longevity through the lens of both Western functional medicine and Eastern holistic practices,” says SHA managing partner Alejandro Bataller, whose father, Alfredo Bataller, was inspired to found the company after integrative medicine and nutritional shifts helped him overcome early stage colon cancer.

All-inclusive rooms at SHA Mexico run $600 to $9,000 a night, plus program rates starting at $4,800 for a four-night stay. In late June, SHA’s umbrella company, AB Living Group, opened St. Regis Costa Mujeres Resort & Residences next door with a luxe spa, 24-hour butler service, daily champagne sabrage and guest access to SHA. For those who want to truly live the lifestyle, private SHA Residences start at $2.5 million. Next up is SHA Emirates (billed as “the world’s first longevity island”), slated to open in AlJurf, along the coast between Dubai and Abu Dhabi, in early 2028. Residences there will cost $27 million.

#675. ‘GTA 6′ Developer Rockstar Games’ Workers Vote Against Union Recognition (Gaming News Roundup)

Employees of “Grand Theft Auto VI” developer Rockstar Games voted against union recognition this week.

In a Nov. 26 vote that included 1,544 staff members (93.2% voter turnout across the Rockstar Games workforce), 75.3% voted against Rockstar Game Workers Union’s recognition with the Independent Workers of Great Britain (IWGB) and 24.7% voted in support.

As a result of the vote, Rockstar Games is not required to recognize the union and regularly engage in collective bargaining with reps. Related Stories Cannes Condemns Five-Year Prison Sentence Against Iranian Palme d’Or Winner Jafar Panahi and Pleads for International Support Sweden’s Oscar Entry 'Adult Supervision' Closes Further Deals (EXCLUSIVE)

“For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society—this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for,” the IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union said in a statement. “Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognize we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.

“We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we’ve built together and the launch of ‘Grand Theft Auto 6,'” Rockstar Games head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe said in a statement.

A Rockstar Games spokesperson added: “This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we’re excited to build on all we’ve accomplished together.”

See more gaming news from the week in the roundup below.

The wait for “Avengers: Doomsday” is almost over, and soon, fans can play in that world in addition to watching the story unfold.

To celebrate the movie hitting theaters Dec. 18, Scopely, in collaboration with Marvel Games, is uniting “Monopoly Go!” with Marvel Studios’ highly anticipated “Avengers: Doomsday” for an all-new season of “Doomsday Go!”

This season, which runs Nov. 25 — Jan. 27, brings new shields, tokens and dice with richer animations and visual effects and visually enhanced super stickers and super tokens.

The “Doomsday Go!” album is packed with 23 unique sticker sets featuring Marvel Super Heroes from Thor and Iron Man to Deadpool, Wolverine, Spider-Man, the X-Men and more. Players can collect super hero team sets, follow story sets, explore whimsical designs and piece together puzzles as Tycoons build a collection worthy of the Marvel Universe.

Wargaming’s “World of Tanks” will feature actor Steve Buscemi as the star of its Holiday Ops 2027, the highly anticipated annual winter celebration across the video game franchise.

Buscemi stars as Coldstone, an observant investigative reporter (and tank enthusiast) who is introduced in a new short film released to promote the “World of Tanks” Holiday Ops season. When the regular anchor is unable to go on air, he takes over the live broadcast just as a series of holiday disasters begins to pile up on screen. Sensing a conspiracy and spotting clues others miss, Coldstone uncovers the truth and saves the holidays. Once the broadcast is over, Coldstone invites players into World of Tanks as a tank commander, ready to set assignments and share festive rewards.

“What I liked about Coldstone is that he doesn’t just go along with the story. He pays attention and has a real eye for detail,” Buscemi said. “I hope World of Tanks players enjoy the retro style, humor, and holiday spirit in the film.”

Lenny Kravitz has been revealed as the new Elusive Target in “HITMAN World of Assassination” reprising the role of his iconic “007 First Light” character, the Pirate King Bawma.

Per IO Interactive (the developer behind both the “Hitman” franchise and “007 First Light”), “In this latest mission, Agent 47 is deployed to Ambrose Island on the instructions of the Pirate King, Bawma. A former child soldier turned ruthless ruler of Aleph, Bawma was last seen in IO Interactive’s Game of the Year nominee 007 First Light, where he commands both fear and respect in equal measure. This time around, Bawma has a rather unconventional assignment for Agent 47, insisting on directing the operation himself and guiding 47 throughout the mission via in-ear dialogue. Once 47 tracks Bawma down through the ruins and jungles of Ambrose Island, it soon becomes clear that something far more valuable than a simple target is at stake. Lenny Kravitz lends both his voice and likeness to his reprisal of Bawma, and the mission brings a bright, upbeat tone and an easy-going holiday feel to World of Assassination.”

The Battle of the Boroughs Minecraft Competition will return to New York City for the fifth consecutive year.

Hosted by New York City Public Schools and the NYC Mayor’s Office of Media and Entertainment (MOME), the competition incentivizes students in grades 3-12 to build a more inclusive and sustainable culture while developing critical thinking, computer science, public speaking and problem-solving skills. This year’s prompt will challenge students to develop Minecraft builds that create a safer, more connected Penn Station neighborhood.

Submissions for elementary, middle and high school teams are now open on the New York City Public Schools website and close Jan. 6.

ITV Studios unveiled on Monday a faithful, nostalgia-packed “Roblox” experience based on the original 1960s TV series “Thunderbirds.”

The game introduces a new generation to the series by recreating the look and spirit of the show, from the famous launch sequences to the craft designs fans grew up with, all with a modern twist.

“Recreating Thunderbirds, such an iconic piece of British television and a treasured brand at ITV Studios, required immense care, passion and dedication,” Ashley Lewis, managing director of Metavision, said. “By pairing the unmistakable DNA and enduring spirit of the 1960s original with Roblox’s rapidly evolving technical capabilities, we’ve been able to bring Tracy Island and its iconic rescues to life with truly impressive scale and fidelity. We hope we’ve created an authentic experience for long-standing fans while introducing a new generation to the excitement and imagination of Thunderbirds.”

#674. Denis Villeneuve “Deeply Disappointed” Disney Put ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Against ‘Dune 3’

The director breaks silence on going head-to-head against Marvel's titan on "Dunesday."

Everybody has found it pretty cute, if slightly baffling, that expected box-office heavyweights Dune: Part Three and Avengers: Doomsday are opening on the same day (Dec. 18).

But Dune franchise director Denis Villeneuve isn’t amused by going head-to-head with the Marvel titan.

Villeneuve explains in a new interview that he was “deeply disappointed” by the “Dunesday” scheduling, but that Warner Bros. was basically trapped in the slot because the studio had successfully secured an exclusive run on IMAX screens for Dune 3 through the December holidays. Related Stories Movies 'Avengers: Doomsday' Eyes $270M Opening as 'Dune: Part Three' Also Heads for Big Start Movies 'Avengers: Doomsday' Final Trailer Shows Major X-Men Moment

“Listen, I will be honest,” he told Time. “The first Dune came out at the end of the pandemic. We made a great box office in a very rough environment. But we had the winds against us. Then the second movie, same thing. We were meant to release in the fall, and we had to release at the end of winter because of the two Hollywood strikes. We had success, but it was not easy. The third time, I said to myself, ‘Finally, there is no pandemic, no strike in sight. We will have a normal release.’ Then Disney put the biggest franchise of all time against us. I’m no fool. Those movies are a mammoth.”

“So I was deeply disappointed,” continued the director. “But we had committed to this date, to IMAX. It was impossible to move. So I accepted my fate, praying to the gods of cinema. Dune is not a mammoth like the Avengers, but it’s a sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower, and I hope we will survive. It could be one of the biggest box-office weekends of all time because of both movies. Am I in competition with the Avengers? Absolutely not. It’s a T. rex. But I stand proud because I think the film delivers.”

Both films have notably broken presales records. Dune: Part Three has reportedly bested Warner Bros. all-time presales record, selling more than $30 million worth of tickets for IMAX screens alone (the studio hasn’t released its own all-theater presales numbers). But Doomsday has recently surpassed $100 million and has received the highest initial opening-weekend forecast in NRG tracking history ($270 million). So there’s no world in which both films aren’t big hits, but also no world in which Doomsday doesn’t clock Dune on opening weekend.

Villeneuve also defended making some significant changes to Dune saga author Frank Herbert’s source material for the third film, particularly in the storyline of Chani (Zendaya). “When you adapt, you kill,” he said. “It is not the book. It is my movie inspired by the book, with tremendous respect … I had the idea to make Chani more of a critic regarding the idea of religious colonization … In the third movie, Chani is still a critic of the choices Paul has made. She believes the Fremen should free themselves. She doesn’t want to harm Paul, but she does want to harm his regime. I would have loved to have taken Frank Herbert for a coffee about these ideas because I think he could have liked them. In the book, Chani is there to give Paul foot massages. It’s a character that has not a lot of firepower.”

#673. Justin Timberlake Explains Why He Was ‘Reluctant’ to Make New Docuseries During ‘Tonight Show’ Interview

The singer told Jimmy Fallon why he was initially hesitant to open up about his private life in the upcoming four-part documentary series.

Justin Timberlake is opening up about what convinced him to share a more personal side of himself in his upcoming documentary.

During an appearance on The Tonight Show on Thursday (Nov. 26), the 45-year-old pop superstar told host Jimmy Fallon that he was initially hesitant to pull back the curtain on his private life for Timberlake, a four-part documentary series premiering on Apple TV on Dec. 11.

“I was really reluctant to do it,” Timberlake told Fallon, noting that he’s always been a pretty private person. But his relationship with director Fisher Stevens eventually helped change his mind, with their conversations encouraging him to open up about parts of his life he hadn’t previously discussed.

“When Fisher first approached me to do this, I was reluctant because I was like, ‘I don’t wanna talk about myself,’” Timberlake continued. But as they continued talking, he found himself “searching for something that was beneath the surface a little more.”

The “Can’t Stop the Feeling!” singer also reflected on how his experiences over the past five years have shaped him.

“You just never know what somebody’s going through, right?” Timberlake said. “And I think I kind of decided, maybe people see my life from the outside and it’s like, ‘Wow!’ But everybody’s going through something, and I think I’ve gone through a lot in the last five years that I feel like has made me a better human and a better father, a better husband, a better friend.”

Timberlake said making the docuseries proved “to be really cathartic,” and he hopes his willingness to be vulnerable will resonate with viewers who may be navigating similar experiences.

“Maybe people see my life from the outside and it’s like, ‘Wow!’ But everybody’s going through something,” the singer said. “Maybe I can be a beacon of light for whoever’s watching.”

The four-part series will feature never-before-seen archival footage, along with interviews with Timberlake’s friends, collaborators and family members. His wife, Jessica Biel, and his mother, Lynn Harless, both appear in a recent teaser for the project.

The first two episodes of Timberlake will premiere Dec. 11 on Apple TV, followed by the third episode on Dec. 18 and the series finale on Dec. 23.

Elsewhere during his Tonight Show appearance, Timberlake celebrated the 20th anniversary of his sophomore solo album, FutureSex/LoveSounds, with a pair of musical medleys performed at New York City’s Rainbow Room. The performances featured some of the set’s biggest hits, including “SexyBack,” “My Love,” “Summer Love” and “What Goes Around…Comes Around.”

Elsewhere during his Tonight Show takeover, Timberlake joined Fallon for a turkey-themed comedy sketch, revived their popular “Camp Winnipesaukee” bit, and teamed up with The Roots for a “History of Party Songs” medley featuring hits from the Spice Girls, Earth, Wind & Fire and others.

Watch Timberlake discuss his Timberlake docuseries in the video below.

#672. Record Store Day Black Friday’s Most Wanted, 2026: Beatles, Noah Kahan, Bruce Springsteen, Prince, Sombr, Billy Joel, Katseye and Other Vinyl Must-Finds

Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic

Record Store Day is back in black. As you likely already know, RSD is a semiannual holiday for vinyl hounds, with the Black Friday edition being a less jam-packed adjunct to the primary event in April — meaning that, this year, for instance, there are “only” 188 titles being released, almost exactly half of the 355 exclusives that were put on sale in the spring event. Even with that lesser amount of limited-edition discs going out onto the shelves, there is truly something for everybody in this list. Or, to put it another way: If you can’t find anything that grabs you in this lineup, then, to quote Leonard Cohen, you don’t really care for music, do ya?

Our best guess is that there will not be utter pandemonium in the indie shops or in the lines outside this Black Friday morning, if only because of the lack of a Taylor, Olivia or Billie title this time. Which does not mean that there will not still be a healthy contingent of young people joining the veteran vinyl geeks in the checkout lines. In an interview published earlier in the week in Variety, RSD co-founder Michael Kurtz said that the majority of customers for Record Store Day events are under 35. That may continue to be the case as this one has titles from hot and/or younger-skewing artists or franchises including Noah Kahan, Katseye, Sombr and the “Wicked” and “Kpop Demon Hunters” films.

That said, boomers are still gonna boom, and they, Gen-X-ers, millennials and others who have a taste for classic rock, soul and jazz — meaning every generation, really — will find something to salivate over in a list of vintage material that includes Bruce Springsteen, Prince, Joni Mitchell, Miles Davis, Billy Joel, Bill Withers, Art Blakey and even a collectible from the Beatles that was added to the list after it was first announced in October.

If you want to see the entire list of 188 vinyl releases (a few of which are also having CD editions made available for the occasion) scroll all the way down. But first, if you will, look at our annotated list of 27 of the titles that we consider most covetable, ranging from Carly Rae Jepsen and Cher EPs to a 10,000 Maniacs boxed set to an expanded version of NRBQ’s classic Christmas album.

14,500 copies on 4x LP; 3,700 copies on 2x CD; black vinyl

Springsteen buffs will not always agree on favorite individual shows from his and the band’s 50-year-plus history, but it’s hard to imagine a single fan not considering the “Born to Run” era to be peak form. or not taking a serious interest in this rendering of a long and loose New Year’s Eve concert at the close of 1975. The only question might be which physical format you want it in, since Sony is offering it for Record Store Day Black Friday in both LP and CD form. The much greater amount of vinyl pressed indicates an obvious consumer preference for vinyl nowadays, but with a concert this length, some may reconsider whether they want to flip sides seven times to get it all and opt for compact disc. Whether you pick up a vinyl slipcase or CD jewel box, there are succinct but sweet liner notes from Erik Flannigan, who points out that, yes, that is the band (except for Bruce) decked out in tuxedos in the photographs in the packaging. Good thing any formality about this wonderful show ends there.

10,000 copies of vinyl 12-inch EP; Alpenglow-colored vinyl

Kahan’s exclusive releases have been among the biggest draws at many recent Record Store Days, which is no surprise, given the ongoing presence of two of his studio albums in the top 10 and stadium tours that sell out instantaneously. Fans will already be familiar with the four songs on this EP — “Lighthouse,” “Staying Still,” A Few of Your Own” and “Orbiter” — since they first appeared as bonus tracks on a digital deluxe edition of his smash “The Great Divide” album (and “Orbiter” is a proper single). But having the four tracks partitioned off into their own separate physical release will be irresistible to diehard stickheads.

It’s not like you’re going to get any songs here that you didn’t already get on the recent “Rubber Soul” 60th anniversary super-deluxe edition… or, for that matter, that you haven’t had access to since 1966. But then, that’s the point: This single LP is a recreation of the exact album that U.S. Beatles fans got in ’66, down to the original stereo mix. But that’s been out of print for a long time… and has never been uin print as a gold-colored record, which is the main novelty here. The good news for Beatles collectors is that it’s been pressed in numbers that fall at the very top end of pressings for Record Store Day; the bad news is that 15,000 still won’t last long.

9,400 copies on 3x vinyl; 2,700 copies on 2x CD; vinyl color is crystal blue curaçao

The Prince estate is really making the most out of the fact that it had a pro-shot film of Prince’s six-month 2006-7 residency in Las Vegas in the can. A film of “3121 Las Vegas Live” will briefly hit the big screen in early December, followed by a Blu-Ray edition for home consumption. In the meantime, if you want a physical manifestation of just the music, Record Store Day participant shops are the place to go. The performance captured here starts at a slow simmer but quickly heats up. Suffice it to say that, after hearing this purely audio version, I’ll be lined up for the movie.

Every time there is a new CD boxed set in the ongoing series of Joni Mitchell archival anthologies, a single live performance from that collection gets broken out to have its own separate LP edition for Record Store Day. No complaints at all about that. This ’72 concert is all Joni, accompanying herself on guitar, piano or dulcimer, all the way to a closing “Circle Game” that does have her suddenly surrounded by a chorus of famous and unfamous friends. Some will prefer Mitchell in her purest early-ish form here, and some may prefer the big band era that followed. But hearing the purity of that voice with an emphasis on the then-recent “Blue” and then-forthcoming “For the Roses” is a knockout experience. The only thing more you could wish for is a gatefold jacket instead of putting both discs in a single sleeve (the product description promises gatefold, but it’s not), or liner notes, but it’s still a handsome-looking as well as -sounding package.

The last Billy Joel live album, released for Record Store Day Black Friday 2025, was “Live From Long Island,” pressed in a quantity of 1,500 copies — and fans are still pissed about that. (Resale copy prices are not completely exorbitant, but they do go for more than $100.) Fortunately, the record company got the message and is putting three times that many of this followup on sale, 4,600, although that still may not completely sate the market for live Joel. It’s a spirited set, from a hyperactive “Angry Young Man” opening forward, recorded Dec. 5, 1976 at Connecticut College for a TV special. It includes 15 never-before-released tracks from either the original live shows or a followup that was done to get better takes for the special. The blurb on the back cover promises that four more tracks will be included in a “Turnstiles” 50th anniversary boxed set coming out next year. But few Joel fans will complain about that wait given the wealth of heretofore unreleased music here.

Boone: 5,000 copies on black and white galaxy vinyl

The Sombr and Benson Boone releases are very similar, in that each is a first-time vinyl issue of the EP that started their major-label careers before they broke a lot bigger with a full album that followed. Bot EPs are also mellower than some of the hit music that followed for these artists — Sombr lives up to his name more here. His EP, at four tracks, is less expansive than Boones, which runs to eight songs, and comes with a 12-by-24 insert that has a poster image on one side and lyrics on the other. Apart from their musical merits, both discs just look fab, pulled out of their sleeves and placed into the wild.

Withers: 2,600 copies on LP; 1,300 copies on CD; LP is black vinyl

Various artists/Sweet Relief: 1,200 copies

Now here’s an unofficial two-fer anyone should think about picking up and turning into a double feature, even if their simultaneous release, coming from different labels, may be coincidental. First, there’s Withers’ own 1974 performance, captured for British TV. You can tell the audio is unedited: Withers is heard telling the studio audience that some of his band members are out sick, and in one case restarting a speech. The relaxed feel carries over to the superlative songs. Meanwhile, I have to give an even more enthusiastic endorsement to a double-LP tribute album put together as a benefit for the Sweet Relief Foundation that includes all-new tracks. I was hoping the great Chris Pierce — one of the closest things we have to a modern-day Withers right now — would be one of the artists chosen, and to my sweet relief, he was, contributing “Better Off Dead.” There are also choice cuts from Rickie Lee Jones, Lady Blackbird, Marilyn McCoo and Billy Davis Jr., Ben Harper and others who know how to mix their own spin on things with takes that feel faithful to Withers’ vibe.

2,600.copies of six-LP boxed set; multiple vinyl colors

Rhino has gotten in the habit of issuing one complete boxed set per RSD event for a renowned artist from the Warner-Elektra catalog of riches, from John Prine to Devo. This one for 10,000 Maniacs, composed of all the albums the group put out before Natalie Merchant split to go solo in 1993, is being seen by fans as a very necessary corrective to the fact that a lot of that stuff has been out of print on vinyl forever. Four studio albums are joined by the pre-fame compendium “Hope Chest” and a newly assembled rarities disc full of delectable covers. Merchant is credited with helping oversee the package, including the design of the physical elements, although the liner notes (which are very good) do not include interviews with her or any of the bandmates who continue to carry on without her. It’s worth noting that all of the albums included except the rarities LP are due to be issued individually early next year, if it’s just one or two you need to pick up. But as a fan from their earliest major-label days, I couldn’t imagine not getting the whole thing right now. A matter of curiosity: All of the box and LP packaging here changes the band’s name to Ten Thousand Maniacs from 10,000 Maniacs (although the numerical usage pops up in the liner notes). Some elements of the album cover art have been changed, along with the band-name logos — it has to be a Merchant thing. But if you pick up the individual issues in a few months, apparently the name and artwork will be as we remember them. (The fact that the albums in this box have different covers is further cemented by the lack of barcodes.) Those peculiarities aside, t’s a great trip down maniacal memory lane.

Jepsen has been nothing but prolific in this era, first issuing “Day and Night” as a hefty double-album, then adding eight additional tracks onto the original 24 for a deluxe edition, “Day and Night (Continued).” that runs to an hour and 55 minutes of material. Some things may be more easily digested in smaller chunks, of course, and this EP — also titled “Day and Night (Continued)” — breaks out those eight fresher tracks and gives them their first appearance in a physical format. Plus, you get still more from her photo shoot at Eagle Rock’s Casa Bianca, the best pizza joint in L.A., and if that’s not reason enough to pick it up, you’ve got eight more.

The previous RSD exclusive editions of the “Wicked” and “Wicked: For Good” sold out so quickly, I never did actually catch a glimpse of either of them in my many store visits. That will probably prove true for this combined set that packages both soundtracks together in a 4-LP set in a slipcase with a poster. (The track list, if accurate as rendered online, leaves out the bonus track that was added onto the original RSD “Wicked” issue.) Good luck hunting this down, unless it turns out every franchise fan was sated by the previous two releases after all, which isn’t likely. It’s gonna be popular.

The first of several releases we’ll mention here produced by “jazz detective” Zefv Feldman is a welcome incursion into the wonderful world of Blakey. It comtbines two previously unreleased performances in Paris, the first from 1963 and sporting famous players like Freddie Hubbard and Wayne Shorter, the second with a different ensemble in ’68. “Moons” were on the band leader’s mind, as the collection includes the two big musical moon shots of the era, “Blue Moon” and “Moon River.” The latter opens the collection and might give Henry Mancini a heart attack if he were still around to have one — it’s like “Moon River” on amphetamines (not speaking literally, friends, just figuratively), and it’s quite a fantastic flood. The liner notes booklet is copious as with almost any Feldman-related release, and even though a CD edition will follow for the general market in a week, it’s always worth picking up the limited-edition vinyl versions of these releases just for the larger type and photographs. And, sure, the wide-open grooves, too.

5,000 copies of 2x LP; on “Third Pyramid Pink” vinyl

I would have taken an interest in a B-52s live set anyway, but this one turns out to be particularly a wowser because of the addition of a three-man horn section that really helps some of the songs rock in an augmented way. Fans may already know this Roseland Ballroom NYC ’82 performance from when it was included in the “Ancient Culture: Mesopotamia Revisited” set, but for those of us who didn’t have that, or anyone who did but just likes a good breakout, it’s a delightful revelation of the band at its early ’80s peak.

3,500 copies of 12-inch vinyl EP; red vinyl

Cher had not released any original material in many years until she came back with a Christmas project that included some songs newly written to add to the holiday tuneage canon. With this EP spinoff, the emphasis is on the dance-ier chestnuts, including three different mixes of “DJ Play a Christmas Song” and an added duet with Kelly Clarkson. The lady-in-red cover shot is different from any previous artwork in her Christmas-music campaign, too.

We were not able to preview this particular release, so we cannot vouch for what the “dance break” versions of three of Katseye’s most popular songs sound like — “Debut,” “Gnarly” and “Gabriela.” But we can tell you the way it will fly off the shelves will be gnarly indeed. All three mixes are congregated on one side of the vinyl, with a mystery etching on the other. Each copy is said to includes two out of six “randomly selected unique photocards,” so fans will be figuring out how to get around the one-copy-per-customer rule in most stores, as if this needed an incentive to sell out faster.

Another archival production from Zev Feldman, who is stretching out from being seen as “just” a jazz guy with his Bobby Womack and Marianne Faithful releases this Record Store Day. Womack can also stretch out, as it turns out, with two numbers in this live set that go past the 12-minute mark, “You’re Welcome, Stop on By” and “Communication” are both over 12 minutes long. Recorded in Paris in 1976, where the liner notes say he was having a higher profile at the time than in the U.S., this collection feels essential as a revelation of just what an expansive showman he was as well as crafter of classic soul singles.

10,000 copies; “Derpy Sussie Splatter” vinyl

The hunt for “Kpop Demon Hunters” collectibles never stops. Record Store Day just had dual editions of the soundtrack that were quick and easy sellouts, but that could hardly stand in the way of yet another version — and surely not the last — this one featuring fresh art created by official “Demon Hunters” production designer Mingjue Helen Chen and visual development artist Marion Bordeyne. We’ll let the product description do the rest of the talking: “This Derpy Sussie Splatter vinyl includes exclusive holographic art on both the front cover and triple gatefold, 3 of 6 mini inserts, 1 of 3 holographic mini inserts, a sticker sheet, and an oversized poster.” You might have to take their word for it since it won’t be surprising if most or all of the copies are gone by the time you get your lazy post-Thanksgiving butt to the shop.

Sax man Getz is the only one with his name above the title on this release, but for the first three of its six sides, legendary guitarist João Gilberto is his equal costar. Together, they recreate the magic they’d made together in a historic studio teaming in one of the few live shows they did together to follow that. All the music here was previously released by Resonance more than a decade ago, but this three-LP set for the first time combines two albums — one of Getz with Gilberto in SF, one without — into an exemplary single package (and the Getz-only half of the equation never made it onto vinyl before). The multiple interviews or essays in the copious liner notes even include a sizable explanation of the bossa nova craze that finds a kind of quiet culmination here.

Fountains of Wayne’s final album before their breakup sometimes gets undervalued because it’s their least comical, most sober outing, perhaps reflecting the more dominant influence of Chris Collingwood, versus the wryer touch favored by Adam Schlesinger, who’d run the show more on the preceding record. Regardless, there’s wit enough here, along with some of the band’s starker songs. It’s been challenging for FoW fans to complete their vinyl collections, since this fast went out of print after a single pressing in 2001. Even now, 2,000 is not a lot, but it’ll be at least enough to satisfy some of us who never stopped believing that this brilliant group had it going on.

This is the “Bitches Brew”-era Miles who took free jazz into the land of psychedelia, if you hadn’t already guessed that from the cover art by his favorite cover painter in the ’60s, Mati Klarwein. It might as well have been recorded at the Fillmore, even though Davis actually had his all-star quintet (Wayne Shorter, Chick Corea, Dave Holland and Jack DeJohnette) in Copenhagen for a TV taping. The music has previously been heard on a DVD and on a one-time vinyl pressing of just a few hundred copies, but this mastering is said to be a revelation even for the relatively small number of cultists who’ve already heard this dynamic performance in some form.

3,500 copies; on “Pawn Shop Patina”-colored vinyl

As the title and cover hint, this is a collection of cover songs these Dolls have done over the years, and what great taste they’ve had in other bands, as evidenced in a collection that runs from the Plimsouls’ “A Million Miles Away” to the Kinks’ “Catch Me Now, I’m Falling,” with stops for Tom Petty, INXS, Prince and… Supertramp! (A CD and digital release will follow a week after this vinyl exclusive.)

5,000 copies; 3D zoetrope picture-disc vinyl

We did not get a review copy of this, but we’re going to guess from the product description alone that it might be fun, with or without actually listening to what’s in the grooves, just from looking at them. “Zoetrope” discs have been a thing for a while, turning vinyl into animation, but this is the first one we can recall seeing that is billed as a 3D zoetrope disc, with cardboard glasses to put on to enjoy the effect. We look forward to hearing whether the effect of watching that is as mind-bending as the Gizzard boys’ music typically is, and what substances it is best combined with.

1,800 copies on three-sided 2x LP set; black vinyl

We’re still morning Faithful’s passing, so it’s moving to hear her in her prime, or one of her primes, in a performance captured in 1983, after a comeback run of three acclaimed albums on Island, including of course “Broken English.” The tape of the D.C. set ends with the title track from that latter album and is missing a few final songs from the actual performance, so it’s spread across three sides and the fourth is devoted to an etching of a William Blake quote in concentric-circle script.

2,215 copies of six-45-rpm-singles boxed set; different marbled color variations

Jazz Dispensary dispenses something worth picking up for every single RSD edition, and this time they’ve eschewed the usual single-LP compilation format to put out a box of singles. It comes in a candy-style box, with six different vintage singles in different but equally delicious-looking colors, plus some glow-in-the-dark 45 adapters as a bonus. As usual, even though the description calls these “jazz,” the music therein leans more toward the funk side of the fence, from Eddie Jefferson’s honestly groovy “Psychedelic Sally” to Patrice Rushen’s kinda-weird “Kickin’ Back.” Obscure but charming singles from Rusty Bryant, Idris Muhammad, Pleasure and Johnny Hammond are also represented. Will you play these a lot, or easily find shelf space for an odd-shaped package? Probably no in both cases, yet it’s kind of irresistible as a hep novelty package nonetheless.

What could be better for celebrating the season than NRBQ’s 1978 “Merry Christmas From NRBQ” EP? Very possibly, a modern expansion of that project that extends it to 19 tracks, 10 of them making their vinyl debut, one (the closing “Auld Lang Syne”) getting its premiere altogether. We weren’t able to preview this package to tell you whether they do or don’t rock out the newly added “Jesus Loves Me” and “The Christmas Song,” but we hope to score a copy and fill in that part of the NRB-FAQ.

For your printout needs, here’s the full list of 2026 Record Store Day Black Friday exclusives, as released in October:

#671. Masaaki Yuasa’s ‘Daisy’s Life’ Unveils First Look Images From Japanese Anime Giant’s Next Feature

The first images from the animated adaptation of Banana Yoshimoto’s novel comes ahead of the movie now scheduled to hit theaters in Japan in 2027.

Japanese anime master Masaaki Yuasa’s new studio, ame pippin, has revealed first look images and a clip from the highly-anticipated animated feature Daisy’s Life, a tale of grief and healing now delayed to a 2027 theatrical release in Japan.

The first title from Yuasa’s new studio ame pippin unveiled images to The Hollywood Reporter of the main characters from the animated adaptation of Banana Yoshimoto’s novel, The Life of Daisy, and original illustrations by Yoshitomo Nara. In one image, the young protagonist Daisy and her closest friend, Dahlia, are standing together in a lush forest. Related Stories Movies Golden Globes Category Chaos: When 'The Drama' Is a Comedy... Movies Golden Globes: 'I Play Rocky' Submitted as Comedy (Exclusive)

The second image shows both animated characters seated together at the roots of a tree, bonding over yakisoba, a Japanese stir-fried noodle dish. Their friendship helps frame the story of Daisy, who, as a child, lost her mother, her only family, in a tragic accident and now grieves that death as she struggles with a new life with her aunt. Studio ame pippin on Thursday unveiled a short clip from Daisy’s Life on X.

“On a long, lonely night during the rainy season, she (Daisy) plays the recorder by herself. As if drawn by the sound, Dahlia appears and becomes the friend who supports Daisy through her isolation. Years later, while Daisy is living and working at her aunt and uncle’s yakisoba restaurant, a letter arrives from Brazil. It speaks of the mysterious connection between two lonely souls separated by distance and time,” a synopsis from the producers of Daisy’s Life states about the young girl’s life changing one sleepless night.

The film is the first animated feature from ame pippin, the animation studio founded by Yuasa in 2025. Daisy’s Life also marks the first animated adaptation of books by Yoshimoto, a popular Japanese writer whose literary work has been published in 30 countries, with over seven million copies in print.

Published in 2000, Yashimoto’s The Life of Daisy novel centers around Daisy (Hinagiku) and explores the themes of death and loss through Daisy’s relationships with her mother and childhood best friend, Dahlia.

Director Yuasa is known for classic films like The Tatami Galaxy and Ping Pong the Animation, and in 2013 co-founded Science SARU with Eunyoung Choi. He directed an episode of Adventure Time and The Night Is Short, Walk on Girl.

Yuasa left Science SARU in 2020 after Keep Your Hands Off Eizouken! and directed Inu-Oh, which earned both Golden Globe and Annie nominations. Character designer Izumi Murakami created the animated characters for Yuasa’s Daisy’s Life adaptation, while production designer Tomotaka Kubo created the film’s settings that envelop Daisy and Dahlia’s time together.

Visual development artist Batiste Perron, color designer Ayaka Nakamura, director of photography Yoshihiro Sekiya and editor Kiyoshi Hirose are also part of Yuasa’s creative team.

The Japanese-French co-production is from ame pippin and Miyu Productions, with Fumie Takeuchi, Emmanuel-Alain Raynal and Pierre Baussaron sharing producer credits.

Yuasa is guest curating the Drawn Universes: Visions in Animation program at the Toronto Film Festival’s Lightbox complex through Dec. 29, and on Friday night will participate in an informal conversation at the festival’s Lightbox facility in Toronto.

#670. The Killers Guitarist Dave Keuning Survived ‘Major Stroke’ With ‘40% Chance of Survival’: ‘I Can Play Guitar Just as Good as Before’

Dave Keuning, guitarist for The Killers, said that he survived a “major stroke” two weeks ago that had a “40% chance of survival” but he’s still able to “play guitar just as good as before.” He revealed the news on Thanksgiving, along with announcing the birth of his daughter.

“Happy Thanksgiving, everyone! Three months ago, we had our baby girl, Odette,” Keuning wrote. “Two weeks ago, I had a major stroke, and thanks to my wife acting fast, I went straight to the hospital and into surgery. The first hour after a stroke is critical when it comes to getting to the hospital. I had a blood clot in my brain that cut off the blood supply to the entire right side of my brain. By the time I arrived at the hospital, I was blind in one eye and had lost function on my left side, but I still wasn’t able to realize I was having a stroke. The doctors said I had a 40% chance of survival and I would have disabilities after, but by some miracle I am fine.” Related Stories Qatar Is Forging Ahead With Film and TV Industry Plan, Undeterred by Regional Turbulence Huw Edwards Channel 4 Doc Slammed by U.K. Prime Minister: 'We Have No Interest in Hearing What He Has to Say'

Keuning thanked his Killers bandmates, including lead singer Brandon Flowers, drummer Ronnie Vannucci Jr. and bassist Mark Stoermer, for their support during his recovery.

“And yes I can play guitar just as good as before,” Keuning wrote. “It was the first thing I checked when I woke up from surgery. I feel extremely fortunate that I am alive and well, and that I can use my hands and feet and talk just like before. I am thankful for my wife, my son, my daughter, and all of my bandmates, who I feel closer to than ever.”

#668. Why the incoming US Congress should ban the development of self-improving AI

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Alex Bores is a US politician in the New York State Assembly in New York City, New York, USA, and a co-founder of AI-safety advocacy group Who Decides.

The recent US midterm elections were a democratic test of the country’s rapid expansion of artificial-intelligence infrastructure. Data centres emerged as a key issue in several election campaigns, and prominent Democrats have outlined policies to strengthen federal regulations on AI once they take office in January.

I am a Democratic politician trained in computer science who stood in a June congressional primary election that attracted millions of dollars from groups backed by the technology industry (I narrowly lost my race). I took one central message from the midterm election results: US voters are unhappy with the industry-led roll-out of AI and want greater control over how the technology is developed and deployed.

Why AI companies can’t be trusted to self-regulate

Why AI companies can’t be trusted to self-regulate

The newly elected US Congress must respond to the popular mood. An immediate priority should be to ban AI systems that can improve themselves without human authorization or oversight. This process, known as recursive self-improvement (RSI), is thought to be close to realization at some frontier AI laboratories. Voters fear that granting such autonomy to the technology would risk surrendering human control over AI altogether.

Most of the major AI companies are already using the technology to automate parts of AI development. Anthropic reported in August that its Claude model assists with more than 90% of the firm’s AI research and development and leads 26% of that work, completing specific tasks under human supervision. OpenAI, meanwhile, notes that its researchers now use more than three days of AI-agent work for every day of human work. And the firm is open about its eventual goal of full automation, including areas in which AI systems could design and build increasingly powerful successors with little or no human oversight.

In my view, this is a dangerous path, particularly because there is enough evidence on what could go wrong when humans lose control of AI agents. In July, some 700 OpenAI agents unexpectedly coordinated to hack into the servers of Hugging Face, another AI firm. In a separate incident in October, AI agents found ways to manipulate the records of their actions, making their behaviour harder for humans to monitor. If AI systems increasingly participate in building their successors, such failures could intensify. (OpenAI has not responded to requests for comment.)

We need a new ethics for a world of AI agents

We need a new ethics for a world of AI agents

The companies are racing each other to market dominance, and against that economic pull, no voluntary norm will stand. Hence, Congress must step in. A ban on fully autonomous RSI would build on a rare area of cross-partisan agreement: individuals from independent senator Bernie Sanders to Republican political strategist Steve Bannon think that humans must remain in control of AI.

To be effective, such a ban must be specific. A person merely clicking ‘approve’ on thousands of AI-proposed experiments each day is not exercising meaningful control. The law should instead prevent AI systems from independently taking consequential steps in AI development, such as launching a training run for a new frontier model or deploying it internally for AI research. One way to do this would be to require a senior executive to certify that qualified human reviewers have examined the proposed changes and relevant safety evaluations before any development actions proceed. Executives should be personally liable for failing to perform oversight duties.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03849-8

A.B. is co-founder of Who Decides, an advocacy group that seeks to shape the policy discussions around AI for the 2028 Democratic presidential field. It will do so by working with local organizations across the early primary and swing states — it will not endorse or spend for specific candidates.
