#667. Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help

Seeing someone break a rule makes people more likely to break it too, a new study has found, especially when the rule-breaker is on their side politically. Watching others behave well barely made a difference.

Most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty. But what happens when the person next to them walks straight across?

A new study suggests they become more likely to follow. In an online experiment led by researchers at the University of Amsterdam, people who saw someone from their own political camp break a rule outright were nearly twice as likely to do the same. Seeing someone follow the rule barely made a difference.

A small number did more than copy. They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched. According to Lucas Molleman, an assistant professor of developmental psychology at the University of Amsterdam who led the research, a few bad actors like these can "basically take off the guardrails of the group."

The researchers wanted to know how seeing other people's choices affects whether someone sticks to a rule. They recruited 750 adults in the United States, roughly half Democrats and half Republicans, a week before the 2024 presidential election.

Participants watched an animated shooting star cross a row of 100 squares and were told to click the square where it shone brightest, which was always near the middle. Squares further to the right paid more money, so there was a reason to cheat.

Each person chose first on their own. They were then shown what a previous participant had done, whether that person had followed the rule, bent it or broken it outright, and which party they supported. Then they could change their answer. The task was repeated six times.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The experiment had no real-world stakes, and nobody was punished for cheating. Other researchers say that matters. "That's not how the world works," Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who was not involved in the study, told Science News.

Punishment and social pressure, he argued, also shape whether rule-breaking spreads.

Rule-breaking spread in the experiment. When people chose on their own, they picked the square furthest to the right, the most lucrative and most blatant violation, about 23% of the time. After seeing someone from their own party make that choice, they did so almost 40% of the time.

Small violations had only a small effect. Blatant ones had a much larger one.

Most people matched what they had seen or stayed below it. But just over 4% went further, breaking the rule by more than the person they had watched.

Good examples had little effect. Seeing a previous participant stick to the rule rarely changed what others did, even when that person was from their own party.

People also differed. Some followed the rule every time and others broke it every time, whatever they saw. The rest shifted depending on what others had done.

People were more likely to copy rule-breaking when it came from their own side. The effects were stronger when the person being watched shared the participant's political leanings.

Not everyone reads that as contagion. Stephen Reicher, a social psychologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland who was not involved in the study, told The Guardian that if influence depends on who the other person is, it does not spread the way a disease does. He pointed out that people who see a riot often turn up afterwards to help clean up.

To see how individual choices might add up, the researchers ran computer simulations. They created a digital version of each participant and placed them in groups of 100.

In some scenarios, the handful of people prone to escalating pushed the whole group toward heavy rule-breaking. But when the simulated groups contained the same share of committed rule followers as the real experiment, rule-breaking leveled off at a moderate level.

Molleman called the work fundamental science and said the real world is far more complex. He sees possible links to situations such as drivers speeding together, or protests that turn violent.

He also said it challenges how people see themselves. In individualist cultures such as the Netherlands and the UK, he said people tend to believe they make their own decisions. But "in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing."

#666. Denis Villeneuve Pledges Traditional, “Unapologetic” Bond: “Not Here to Change the DNA”

The director teases a classic approach to his Amazon MGM film starring Robert Pattinson: "I love the way the character behaves."

Denis Villeneuve says his highly anticipated reboot of the James Bond franchise isn’t going to back away from the “unapologetic” traits of the iconic character.

The Dune: Part Three director teased his vision of 007 in a new interview and suggested that he’s a traditionalist when it comes to portraying Ian Fleming’s suave, seductive, killer spy.

“I love traditions,” Villeneuve told Time. “I love the unapologetic way the character behaves, the panache. I’m not here to change the DNA of James Bond. I’m here to embrace it, to bring it to the world of today. I’m a hardcore James Bond fan, and I want other fans to have fun watching my film. Of course, it will be tainted by my sensibility. But I wake up every morning with a stupid smile because it’s a world of pure cinematic pleasure.” Related Stories Movies 'Twilight' Director Reveals Robert Pattinson Inspired James Bond Line in 2008 Film: "We Were Seeing the Future" Movies 'Avengers: Doomsday' Eyes $270M Opening as 'Dune: Part Three' Also Heads for Big Start

That said, the director added, “I don’t want to talk too much about Bond because it’s still in the oven cooking. This stage of the process is my favorite part because everything is possible.”

The comments are interesting because of the cultural debate that’s surrounded Bond in recent years, and how the later Daniel Craig films attempted to wrestle with the question of how the often sexist cinematic character dating back to the 1960s should operate in the modern age.

How much Villeneuve was thinking of Pattinson during his comments is unclear — the interview was conducted one week before The Batman actor was publicly announced as the new Bond.

Meanwhile, speculation has shifted to who will play the film’s villain, with oddsmakers thinking Tom Hardy has a strong shot (indeed, given Pattinson’s slight frame, choosing a physically imposing villain would make for a nicely formidable antagonist). Director Danny Boyle — who was originally tapped to direct No Time to Die — has said that “beginning to talk about Jack O’Connell as a possible villain.” O’Connell was previously considered a contender to play Bond himself.

Boyle told The Alchemy podcast that both Pattinson and O’Connell have a similar quality. “They have that thing [where] you want to watch them,” he said. “And it’s impossible to quantify what it is; otherwise we’d all buy it for ourselves. But it’s just there and you want to follow them.”

#664. Goo Goo Dolls Fans Slam NBC Over Thanksgiving Halftime Show Snub: ‘Badly Handled’

The network aired just 90 seconds of the band's performance in favor of Aaron Rodgers coverage.

Goo Goo Dolls fans are outraged after NBC cut short the band’s Thanksgiving Day halftime performance.

The network is facing backlash after airing just 90 seconds of the John Rzeznik-fronted group’s nine-minute set during Thursday’s (Nov. 26) Buffalo Bills-Kansas City Chiefs game.

The Goo Goo Dolls performed “Iris,” “Slide” and “Broadway” in the pouring rain at Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, New York, just outside the group’s hometown of Buffalo. NBC aired only a portion of “Iris” before cutting away to an interview with NBC commentator Mike Tirico and former Pittsburgh Steelers coach Mike Tomlin about quarterback Aaron Rodgers, who had recently been released by the team.

“They are a great band. That was badly handled and disrespectful,” musician and actor Stevie Van Zandt wrote on X.

NBC Sports PR promoted the Tomlin interview on social media about an hour before kickoff, but many viewers weren’t happy with the network’s decision.

“The fact that NBC won’t show Goo Goo Dolls in the rain in Buffalo is despicable,” one person wrote on X. Another added, “NBC only aired the last 30 seconds. Wasting time on useless clown Rodgers.”

A third wrote, “No one give a f#@k about a washed up Rodgers amd the dumpster fire he has left in Pittsburgh outside of Pittsburgh. @NBCsports should be embarrassed! Every other game on the other networks showed the entirety of the halftime shows but @NBC was amateurish by showing nonsense.”

Unlike the Goo Goo Dolls, Thanksgiving’s other halftime acts — Wu-Tang Clan on CBS and Miranda Lambert on Fox — had their performances aired in full during their respective game broadcasts.

The Goo Goo Dolls hadn’t publicly commented on the situation at press time. Billboard has reached out to the band’s representatives for comment.

#663. How This Year’s Black Friday Deals Explain the Tumultuous State of Streaming

There's a method to the discount madness, and the deals quietly signal where corporate priorities lie.

The streaming business is in flux, and Black Friday deals can help explain it.

It’s not hyperbole: Netflix stock has been cut in half from its all-time high. Bundles are proliferating. And Skydance CEO David Ellison has made it clear that a merger of HBO Max and Paramount+ is a question of when, not if.

Black Friday streaming deals are an annual tradition at this point, but given the state of the business, they can also shed light on how the entertainment giants behind them are thinking about the future of their products.

HBO Max and Paramount+ are offering very different types of deals, even as their parent company Skydance, is actively preparing for a discount bundle set for early next year, and with a full merger of the services following later on

HBO Max is offering an aggressive 50 percent discount on its ad-supported tier, charging $5.49 per month for a full year. Paramount+, meanwhile, is offering both its premium and standard plans for $2.99 per month, albeit only for the first two months.

With the bundle imminent and a merger coming (expect Paramount+’s tech stack to win out over HBO Max’s), the Black Friday deals are a last gasp before what is expected to be an aggressive discount campaign early next year.

The biggest new streamer to launch in the last year, Fox One, is offering a steep 75 percent discount, $5 for the first month, before it reverts back to $20 in month two.

Peacock, meanwhile, is offering generous discounts on both its select and premium plans, selling them for $2.99 and $8.99 per month for the first three months.

Disney, which has been leaning into bundles, is offering a year of Disney+ and Hulu for $5 per month, hoping to get viewers hooked on its two entertainment platforms (ESPN is the other) ahead of a full sunset of the Hulu standalone app (it is expected to continue as a standalone service within Disney+).

Apple TV, which is still trying to gain the scale that many of the other services already have, is offering an aggressive discount of over 50 percent, selling six months of the services for $6.99 per month, down from its typical price of $14.99 per month.

And niche streamers are being more aggressive: Look at Starz, which is offering an astonishing deal: $11.99 for 12 months, putting the price at under $1 per month when buying the annual plan (a more modest discount is available on monthly plans), underscoring how it needs to gain scale, and fast. Crunchyroll, Sony’s anime-focused streamer, is also offering discounts of over 50 percent for six months, ranging from $3.99 for its base tier to $8.99 for its ultimate tier.

And it’s a world where Netflix, the king of the crop, still feels as though it has no need to offer discounts of any sort. After all, when you have won the subscription streaming war, it’s better to keep those margins intact.

#662. ‘Summer Meadow’ Directors Confront ‘Hypocrisy’ in Films About Migrants: ‘It’s as Though Black and Arab People Are Forbidden to Dream’

The seemingly unremarkable movement of flocks of sheep across the French Alps took on a deeper significance for filmmakers Naël Khleifi and Lisa Debauche. The animals could freely cross borders that certain human beings could not.

That observation was among the starting points for “Summer Meadow,” which explores migration, the complexities of exile and the universal desire to discover the world against a backdrop of the quiet rhythms of pastoral life. Related Stories Cannes Condemns Five-Year Prison Sentence Against Iranian Palme d’Or Winner Jafar Panahi and Pleads for International Support ‘Paper Tiger’ Director James Gray Calls Out ‘Dumb, Ethically, Morally Bankrupt’ Festival Competitions and Jokes That He’s Giving Up on Cannes: ‘I’ve Learned My Lesson’

“There are shepherds in Lebanon, in Palestine, in France. They’re everywhere,” Debauche says. “There’s something in that timelessness that allowed us to question contemporary issues without confining the film to current events.”

Following an award-winning run at Locarno and the Cairo Film Festival, the Belgian-French feature screened at the Doha Film Festival in the Ajyal Feature Film Competition, judged by a youth jury. The film follows Hana (Manal Issa), a young Lebanese apprentice shepherdess who seeks refuge in the French Alps. Her encounters with fellow shepherdess Lisa (Sibylle Bataille) and a Moroccan migrant, Kebir (Elkebir Belfatmi), gradually draw her out of her isolation.

For Khleifi, a Belgian-Palestinian filmmaker whose 2021 documentary “Alpes” followed residents and activists secretly helping migrants cross the French-Italian border by night, pastoral life offered another means of exploring migration, freedom and the exploitation of humans and nature.

In challenging conventional narratives of migration, Khleifi identified with Kebir’s journey, driven as much by curiosity and a desire to discover the world as by a search for economic opportunities. “It’s something I know from within,” he tells Variety. “My father’s desire to leave Palestine came from a place that pushed him to leave for many reasons, but also from a desire to discover the world.”

Khleifi contrasts the portrayal of European immigrants in Western cinema with that of Black and Arab migrants. “It’s as though Black and Arab people are forbidden to dream. It drives me crazy,” he says, exasperated. “At some point, we have to turn the question back on the West and confront its hypocrisy. This film is a cry. We’re human beings too. Everyone has the right to dream.”

“Each story is different and rich, each journey, each feeling experienced, each past,” adds first-time director Debauche. “We so often put people into categories. We shut them in boxes, and with this film we wanted to break those boxes open.”

The filmmakers also sought to blur the boundaries between documentary and fiction. “In ‘Alpes,’ I tried to break away from the conventions of documentary filmmaking, particularly the way migration is so often depicted,” Khleifi explains. “Here, I thought to myself, ‘We’re going to make a fiction film using the techniques of documentary.’ It’s a continuation of my cinematic exploration.”

Though meticulously written, the screenplay continued to evolve throughout production. During 10 days of preparation before filming, conversations with Issa helped deepen Hana’s character, while Debauche encouraged first-time actress Bataille to move beyond scripted dialogue and speak in her own words.

Those exchanges, Debauche notes, gave the film an added measure of soul. “We can spend months, years writing, trying to get as close as possible to a character. But reality is always much stronger than fiction.” She goes on, “Our conversations brought us so much, shifted something in us, too, and contributed to the depth of the characters and the story.”

The filmmakers also resisted the temptation to explain their characters’ every motivation. “There’s something beautiful about leaving certain things unexplained,” observes Debauche. “It allows viewers to bring their own questions to the film and find their own meaning in the story.”

Hana’s search for refuge, in Khleifi’s view, reflects a broader sense of unease that characterizes modern life. “With the climate crisis, wars, the far right, capitalism and this collective anxiety, we’re all a little messed up,” he says. “Everyone is trying to find a place where they can come up for air.”

Before joining the project, Issa had grown disillusioned with the film industry’s response to the war in Gaza and began questioning whether she wanted to continue making films.

“In films, we’re always talking about human beings. All of a sudden, children are dying in atrocious ways and we don’t want to talk about it anymore,” Issa laments. “I found myself asking why I was doing this. Had I spent years of my life doing a job where you’re afraid to say, ‘Stop killing children’?”

“Summer Meadow” gave Issa both the freedom to express herself and an opportunity to rethink her craft. Working alongside nonprofessional actors and the flocks of sheep allowed her to relinquish control, an experience she likens to an acting workshop, adding that she would carry those lessons into future projects.

“With the sheep, you can’t say, ‘Now I’m going to position myself like this,’” she explains. “I wanted to be out of control. For me, acting is being.”

Having left Lebanon for France at 13, Issa found herself reconsidering her own relationship with freedom through conversations with Belfatmi about his experience of migration. “For me, I had been torn away from my country. All I wanted was to come back,” she recalls. “But had I really experienced life?”

As Khleifi and Debauche edited the film in Europe, Issa was in Beirut amid the Israeli bombardment of the Lebanese capital, a reality that informed their decision to close the film with images of Lebanon.

The friendship between Hana and Lisa, Debauche believes, speaks to the importance of being genuinely available to others. “I think it’s through our encounters with others that we perhaps come closer to ourselves,” she reflects. “These two women have very different stories. At first glance, apart from the sheep and their work, what could they possibly share? And yet, a sense of trust develops between them that allows them to make peace with certain things.”

Issa experienced that firsthand. Increasingly isolated since the onset of the war, she found solace in her friendship with the filmmakers. Debauche encouraged her to share her experiences, both in conversation and on paper, some of which found their way into the screenplay.

“I lived through the same thing Hana did. That’s what’s beautiful. The film came at the right time in my life. It was as though Lisa Debauche was for me what Lisa in the film was for Hana. It opened me up, made me speak out more.”

#659. Monica Bellucci on Challenging Hollywood Ageism in James Bond, Working With Mel Gibson and the Power of Onscreen Nudity: ‘It’s Like a Costume That Brings a Role to Life’

Monica Bellucci, the glamorous Italian star who broke through internationally with “Malena” and “Irreversible,” was 50 when she made James Bond history as the oldest woman to play a Bond girl in Sam Mendes’ “Spectre.”

But rather than marking the twilight of her career as a Hollywood sex symbol, the movie ushered in a new chapter for Bellucci whose career has been enjoying a second wind in recent years. Related Stories Iranian Activist and 'It Was Just an Accident' Screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian Arrested in Tehran on Charges of 'Anti-Government Propaganda' Asha Bhosle and S. Janaki Remembered by Singer K.S. Chithra and Suhasini Maniratnam at IFFI's Lata Mangeshkar Talk

During a candid, wide-ranging masterclass moderated by Variety at the Marrakech Film Festival, Bellucci recalled that Mendes really “wanted to show a mature woman, and I thought it was a beautiful idea.” “He told me, ‘Listen, I have a strong and unusual role that’s going to be surprising, a little revolutionary,” she said. “I was 50, and I had never seen a 50-year-old Bond woman. So I think I’m the oldest James Bond woman, lady or girl that we’ve ever seen,” Bellucci said with a laugh in front of a huge crowd of locals and film students who queued for over two hours to get in.

Ultimately, “Spectre” and Emir Kusturica’s “On the Milky Road,” in which she starred opposite the Serbian filmmaker, came at a pivotal moment in her life.

“Suddenly, I had two very strong roles. Those two films helped me get through the transition of turning 50, which wasn’t easy for an actress,” she said.

Bellucci, whose body of work has largely been shaped by celebrated male auteurs — from Francis Ford Coppola to Giuseppe Tornatore, Gaspar Noé and David Lynch — also noted that she has enjoyed working with more female directors in recent years. She cited Alice Rohrwacher with her Cannes-prizewinning “The Wonders,” Rebecca Miller with “The Private Lives of Pippa Lee,” Kaouther Ben Hania with “The Man Who Sold His Skin” and Léa Mysius’ “Birthday Girl,” which competed at this year’s Cannes.

“When I was younger, there weren’t as many female directors as there are today. It’s new to have so many female directors, screenwriters and even technicians on a set, so many women. We’re witnessing something completely new,” she said.

“It’s another way of telling stories, sometimes another vision. And between women, sometimes there’s this ‘je ne sais quoi,’ as we say in France. Suddenly, we look at each other and, without words, we express ourselves and we understand each other. So I also really like working with women whenever possible.”

Bellucci said the roles she is being offered have also evolved as she’s gotten older, allowing her to explore facets of herself that she couldn’t have accessed earlier in her career.

“Our body is our working instrument. So the instrument changes and, consequently, the roles change. It’s another part of ourselves that’s expressing itself,” she said. “As we get older, we also gain experience, and we have another way of telling the story of life.”

Bellucci, who made her debut on stage in 2019 with the solo show “Maria Callas: Letters and Memoirs” — which she toured in different countries and played in French, Italian and English — said she felt lucky that “times have changed and there’s a lot of respect for women in cinema.”

“In the ’40s, ’50s and ’60s, it was very difficult for a woman over 40 to have a career, even if she was very talented and still had everything it took. And today that has changed.” She cited Susan Sarandon, Judi Dench, Jamie Lee Curtis and Meryl Streep as actors who have paved the way for women to continue playing compelling roles as they age. “There are magnificent actresses who are absolutely fearless,” she said, singling out Streep. “She’s so fearless and she’s incredible. There are several actresses who are free in that sense.”Bellucci also reminisced about her defining role in Giuseppe Tornatore’s 2000 drama “Malena,” which earned two Oscar nominations. Bellucci plays a young woman whose beauty triggers desire and eventually violence in a small Sicilian town during World War II.

Bellucci, who says she was already a film buff from a young age “watching three films a day,” had met the Oscar-winning director of “Cinema Paradiso” during her modeling years in Italy and worked with him on a commercial for Dolce & Gabbana. Four years later, while Bellucci was shooting “Under Suspicion” with Gene Hackman and Morgan Freeman, Tornatore called to offer her the lead role which he wrote for her.

“The script was already very powerful because it tells the story of women living in a man’s world, the difficulty of those relationships, the violence. It’s about a woman who finds herself alone in a man’s world and has to deal with it. Ultimately, it’s still a very contemporary film,” she said.

At the time, Bellucci had already broken through in France with “L’Appartment,” starring opposite Vincent Cassel, and “Malena” represented a daring role which required a great deal of nudity and some intimate scenes with a teenage actor. She said approached these scenes “very naturally.”

“I came from fashion, so I had a freedom with my body that came from the work I had done before,” Bellucci said. “Even today, I think nudity can serve to bring a character to life. When I see films like ‘Anora’ or ‘Poor Things,’ these are films where the actresses’ bodies are very important in bringing the characters to life.”

“When you play a role, if nudity is part of that role, it’s simply a working tool. It’s not a way of exposing yourself. In fact, it’s like a costume that brings a role to life.”

During the conversation, Bellucci also talked about her experience shooting Mel Gibson’s highly controversial blockbuster “The Passion of the Christ,” in which she portrayed Mary Magdalene.

“I had another action film at the same time, and I chose ‘The Passion of the Christ’ because I wanted to work with Mel Gibson. I’d seen films of his that I liked, and it was an experience I wanted to have.”

She said she had no regrets about making the 2004 biblical epic, which sparked controversy over its graphic violence and portrayal of Jewish figures, and went on to gross over $611 million worldwide.

“I think every time a film sparks a discussion, it means it was important to make it. Because discussing and exchanging ideas — that’s the power of cinema,” she said.

She said she approached the role Mary Magdalene as “a simple, human woman who experiences something greater than herself, something she can’t really explain. There is a form of spirituality in everyone.” Although the film didn’t bring her closer to her Catholic upbringing, she said she felt “there is never anything bad in religions. It’s the political use of religion that is dangerous.”

Bellucci also praised Gibson for being “really incredible with actors on set” and revealed she had talked to him about the two-part follow up, “The Resurrection of the Christ,” which he’s currently filming. “Yes, we spoke,” she said of the sequel, adding: “I think he’s a great director.”

During the masterclass, Bellucci also revisited the memorable scene in “The Matrix Reloaded” in which her character, Persephone, demands that Neo — played by Keanu Reeves — kiss her as if he were kissing Trinity (Carrie-Anne Moss) in exchange for her help.

Asked whether she had to do numerous takes of the kissing scene with Keanu Reeves, Bellucci quipped, “It’s not tiring, is it? You can do it.”

“He’s someone who is very gentle, respectful. We met on ‘Dracula’ and saw each other again years later on ‘The Matrix,’“ she said of Reeves.

Despite landing supporting roles in several Hollywood movies at the height of her international breakthrough, Bellucci said she never felt the desire to relocate to the U.S.

“I like America. I love all these possibilities, all this energy, the possibility of making big films as well as independent films. And I like going there. But I feel profoundly European. I live between Paris and Rome, and I love that,” she said.

“The more time passes, the more I realize that I adore my profession and I still have that passion. But I also love the real things in my life. I love having my friends, I love my family. I also love having a kind of everyday life, something that keeps me connected to something real,” she said. “I like cinema, but I prefer life.”

Among her more recent Hollywood outings was Tim Burton’s “Beetlejuice Beetlejuice,” in which she plays Delores, Beetlejuice’s vengeful, soul-sucking ex-wife who comes back from the dead to hunt him down.

Bellucci said Burton’s drawings of Delores helped her envision the character. “He expresses so many things through his drawings and he had made a magnificent drawing of this character. I was already really inspired by that,” she said.

“With all her scars, Delores is a bit of a parody of existence, a metaphor for life,” she said, adding that the role necessitated three hours of makeup every day. “We all have scars. We have to face them, continue to live with them and move forward.” Speaking of the scene in which she reassembles her body, she said “there were special effects, but it was also a bit like a a macabre dance.”

Bellucci, who also worked with Ben Hania and Moroccan-Belgian directing duo Adil El Arbi and Bilall Fallah on “Seven Dogs,” was also upbeat about the new generation of Arab filmmakers.

“There’s a lot happening. This festival is proof of that, isn’t it? All these first and second films, these incredible young filmmakers, beautiful films like ‘Adam’ and ‘The Blue Caftan.’ Beautiful things are reaching international audiences, the Cannes Film Festival and beyond. Long live cinema!“

She concluded the masterclass with a rallying cry for the moviegoing experience. “I hope cinema will never disappear because I truly believe in cinema as one of the cultural elements that are essential to humanity,” she said.

#658. Ben Stiller Says Ariana Grande Exceeded His Expectations in ‘Focker-in-Law,’ Would Do a Fifth ‘Meet the Parents’ Film

The actor also tells The Hollywood Reporter about filming a musical scene in front of the pop star and whether there's more story to tell in the 26-year-old franchise.

Ariana Grande was the newest addition to the Focker family this Thanksgiving.

Following a 16-year gap since the last film in the Meet the Parents franchise, Little Fockers, hit theaters, a fourth installment, Focker-in-Law, was released this week by Universal and Paramount Pictures. Grande stars as Olivia, a former FBI hostage negotiator who accompanies her boyfriend Henry Focker (Skyler Gisondo), the son of Greg Focker (Ben Stiller), to a family reunion celebrating his grandfather Jack’s (Robert De Niro) 80th birthday.

Grande’s performance has received raves, including from The Hollywood Reporter, where critic Frank Scheck called her “the best thing in the film, going toe-to-toe with her more cinematically experienced co-stars and displaying both formidable steeliness and deadpan comic skills.” Stiller, who shares multiple scenes with Grande as his character attempts to sabotage Henry’s proposal to Olivia throughout the film, wasn’t surprised by the Grammy winner’s acting chops. Related Stories Movies 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Devouring $85M Over Thanksgiving Weekend as 'Focker-in-Law,' 'Hexed' Launch Music Ariana Grande Says "Insane Perception" of "Petal" Music Video Felt Like 'Black Mirror' and Intention Was "Me Sharing a Vulnerable Thing"

“I thought she was incredible in Wicked. I was pleasantly surprised by how incredible an actor she is to work with, and I wasn’t not expecting that, but she really surpassed all my expectations in terms of her sense of timing, her character and being able to pull off a character like this. It’s very specific,” he told THR of Grande, who’s returned to acting, alongside her music career in recent years, earning an Oscar nomination for best supporting actress at the 97th Academy Awards for Wicked. “She was great to work with and she’s just a really nice person and fun to hang out with.”

Stiller also recalled one scene that put him in an interesting position: performing in front of the pop star. One of Greg’s attempts to stop Henry from proposing comes when he serenades his father-in-law, Jack, in front of the whole family, singing John Legend’s “All of Me” — the song Henry intended to sing to Olivia before popping the question.

“She was on set watching the whole time and she was incredibly generous and sweet and very supportive. I knew if I tried my best, it probably would be good enough for the movie,” Stiller said with a laugh. “But it was interesting because I had to do it a lot in front of her. It was an interesting day.”

Beanie Feldstein, who plays Henry’s sister Samantha, also had high praise for Grande. “Ari is the most incredible person on planet Earth. I love her more than life itself, and she’s a tour de force in this movie,” she said.

As the Fockerverse has spanned 26 years, Stiller isn’t convinced that John Hamburg’s Focker-in-Law will be the end of the franchise, though he’s leaving that decision up to audiences. “I think if the audience wants one, there is probably another story there,” he said.

And it were up to Stiller? “I would do it for sure,” he quipped.

Focker-in-Law is now playing in theaters.

#657. Sebastian Stan Says ‘Thunderbolts’ Had ‘More Nuance’ Than ‘Some of the Recent’ Marvel Movies and Was a ‘Success’ Despite Disappointing Box Office

Marvel veteran Sebastian Stan is sticking up for last year’s “Thunderbolts,” despite it being one of the lowest-grossing MCU movies.

In the team-up movie, he reprised his role as Bucky Barnes, aka the Winter Soldier, alongside Florence Pugh as Yelena Belova and David Harbour as the Red Guardian to form the Thunderbolts, a new group in the MCU. They later renamed themselves the New Avengers, made up of Wyatt Russell as U.S. Agent, Lewis Pullman as Sentry and Hannah John-Kamen as Ghost, and the team will return in next month’s “Avengers: Doomsday.” Related Stories John Travolta Didn’t Recognize Himself as Alleged JFK Assassin Johnny Roselli in ‘November 1963’: ‘I Went, "Oh My God, He’s the Devil"’ Gérard Depardieu to Stand Trial for Rape Charges After Failed Appeal

After releasing in May 2025, “Thunderbolts” ended its box office run with $382 million worldwide, ranking as the fifth lowest total out of all 38 MCU films. The only movies below it are “Black Widow” ($379 million), “Captain America: The First Avenger” ($370 million), “The Incredible Hulk” ($264 million) and “The Marvels” ($206 million). They’re all a far cry from this summer’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” which is the second biggest MCU movie with $2.5 billion (behind the highest-grossing film ever, “Avengers: Endgame” with $2.94 billion).

“I think it’s just when you’ve had a studio and you’ve had Marvel and it’s been so many years where they’ve just been knocking it out of the park, $350 million global, something like that, it just suddenly doesn’t seem that much,” Stan said on “Next Best Picture.” “But it’s insane how much money that is.”

He added, “For us, it felt like a success. I know a lot of care went into that and it had more nuance to it in terms of some of the recent ones, from my point of view at least, dealing with real issues like mental health and depression and so on.”

“Thunderbolts” was praised by fans and critics for its darker tone and how it elevated its cast of misfit, lesser-known characters. Its director, Jake Schreier, was tapped by Marvel to helm its 2028 “X-Men” movie, with a cast including Sadie Sink, Adam Driver, Inde Navarrette, Kit Connor and more.

#656. Germany news: Metalworkers go on strike as pay dispute heats up

Germany's biggest union is calling for more strikes over heated pay disputes with car makers like Mercedes and shipyards among the companies impacted. Meanwhile, a Berlin hospital fire leaves many injured.

This blog is now closed. Read below for more on these stories and all other things Germany on Monday, November 23.

Thank you for following our coverage of headlines from Germany on Monday, November 24.

The Federal President’s latest major trip takes him to Africa. Frank-Walter Steinmeier has just visited the Ivory Coast and is continuing on to Ghana and Kenya. His goal: to encourage more German companies to invest in Africa.

Frank-Walter Steinmeier has visited 31 African countries during his political career. Even as foreign minister, he traveled regularly to the continent; as federal president, he has made twelve trips so far.

From early on, he viewed Africa not only through the lens of development aid and humanitarian support, but also — much like former Chancellor Angela Merkel — as a market for the German economy that has been underutilized thus far. In 2015, as foreign minister in the Merkel administration, Steinmeier played a central role in the creation of the German-African Economic Summit.

On his current trip as well, Steinmeier is advocating for greater German engagement in Africa. In Abidjan, the capital of the Ivory Coast, following a meeting with Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara, he called on German companies to step outside their comfort zone and take greater advantage of the opportunities offered by the country and the continent.

The Ivory Coast is considered a location with growing potential. Despite its proximity to the Sahel region, which is plagued by terrorism, the country is relatively stable politically. The economy is growing by about six percent annually. Germany has more intensive trade relations with the Ivory Coast than with any other country in sub-Saharan Africa, and nowhere else in sub-Saharan Africa do so many people learn German — an advantage for German small and medium-sized enterprises — all of which both presidents emphasized very clearly during their meeting in Abidjan.

Up next, Steinmeier is scheduled to visit Accra, Ghana, for the sixth German-African Economic Summit, where more than 600 business representatives are expected to attend. As the summit’s initiator, the Federal President will open the event together with the host, Ghanaian President John Mahama. He will be accompanied by a ten-member business delegation representing industry, the financial sector, and energy consulting.

The Economic Summit is taking place at a time when Germany’s relations with African countries are undergoing fundamental changes. In light of geopolitical shifts, Africa is increasingly coming into focus as an economic and trade partner.

The continent’s share of German foreign trade currently stands at just under 2%, or around €30 billion. At the same time, German exports to Africa are rising by at least 6% annually. And since Germany’s economy aims to reduce its dependence on China in the future, opportunities in Africa are growing.

From Ghana, Frank-Walter Steinmeier will travel on to Kenya, the final stop on his tour of Africa.

Environment Minister Carsten Schneider on Monday vowed that Germany will continue to move away from burning fossil fuels despite the failure of the COP31 declaration in Antalya, Turkey, this weekend.

Speaking at an event in Potsdam, Schneider said: "We will clearly maintain our course on climate protection in Europe and Germany, but above all one that makes us independent of oil and gas because otherwise we are vulnerable to blackmail and our economic performance becomes extremely volatile."

Schneider expressed disappointment less at the result of the two-week conference than its format, which he said was far more focussed on spectacle than substance.

Speaking of his vision for a format for future climate conferences, Schneider said: "Basically, I don't need so many people there. What I need are the relevant decision makers with whom I negotiate and make decisions."

Although he voiced relief that the final document from the conference had not represented a step backwards — as well as stressing that some 30 countries had pledged to maintain the move away from fossil fuels — Schneider acknowledged that it had been nearly impossible to find consensus with Russia and Saudi Arabia at the table.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius urged calm over reports that Russia was planning to launch a nuclear-armed satellite into space as early as next month.

"First of ​all, ‌let's remain calm, because there are reports — that's true — but ‌it's ​not clear what kind of weapons these are, and the ​effect they might have depends, in ⁠turn, ​on where they ​are deployed," Pistorius told ​reporters in ‌Berlin.

"Therefore, it's too early to ​speculate ⁠publicly about this. We are consulting ⁠internally ​and taking the necessary measures."

German public broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung first reported on the matter, which said that internal intelligence reports circulated among NATO countries earlier this month said that Russia was ready to bring the alleged satellite, named Sputnik-S, out of storage in Moscow.

The reports said Russia may be planning to launch it as soon as December.

Nuclear weapons are banned in orbit by the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, of which Moscow is a signatory.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said not allowing Ukraine intoNATO in 2008 was a mistake.

At the2008 summit in Bucharest, Romania, German Chancellor Angela Merkel and French President Nicolas Sarkozy argued that they weren't ready to extend NATO membership to Ukraine.

US President George W. Bush said he was in favor of having Ukraine enter into NATO.

But both Germany and France said that that would hurt relations with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The NATO summit then decided that Ukraine would eventually join the alliance, but offered no timetable.

At a press conference on Monday, Merz was asked about whether he thinks the time was right to talk about Ukraine's membership in NATO.

To which Merz said, "If it [Ukraine] had become a member of NATO, this war could probably have been prevented."

Merz meant Russia's war against Ukraine when he said "this war" at the press conference after a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.

Angela Merkel defended her decision at the Bucharest summit as of 2024 as well, saying a large proportion of the Ukrainian population had opposed joining NATO at the time.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called on Russia to end its "dangerous provocations" after two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland on Friday.

Merz delivered those remarks after having met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin on Monday.

"Poland can count on our full solidarity. And if necessary, NATO will of course defend every inch of allied territory," Merz said.

Merz said Europe and NATO must strengthen their defenses.

Drones have repeatedly strayed into NATO airspace in the year since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The incident also came at a time as Poland was hosting a two-week military exercise by Ukraine's allies.

German startup investments in fields such as robotics and defense are set to almost triple this year, a study noted on Monday.

The German Start-up Association and the Joachim Herz Foundation study predicted that investments in so-called "deep tech startups" will surge from just €2.9 billion ($3.17 billion) last year to 8.1 billion ($8.9 billion) this year.

The study described the rise as a "major success for Germany as a business location."

"Deep tech" typically refers to developing cutting-edge technologies based on scientific research, such as AI, biotechnology and quantum computing.

A handful of massive fundraising rounds by firms including humanoid robot developer Neura Robotics,  AI drone maker Helsing and defense tech group Quantum Systems drove the investment boom.

The study also showed about 300 new deep tech startups are expected to be founded this year, a 40% rise compared with last year.

Newly found startups tend to be founded around economic hubs like Berlin and Hamburg, which are also home to leading universities and research institutes.

The study also highlighted challenges, including limited funding compared with their US counterparts and insufficient support to move startups from the laboratory to the real world.

Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

They said that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.

More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.

Similar reports have also emerged to the north of Germany, in Denmark.

As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools."

Read more about the disruptive incidents that have targeted Europe in recent weeks.

Germany's Freie Wähler (Free Voters) party have chosen a new chairman, weeks after their former front man Hubert Aiwanger unexpectedly passed away on November 4.

The party announced on Monday that Bavaria's Digital Affairs Fabian Mehring is to succeed Aiwanger both as party leader on the federal level and as one of two co-chairs of the Bavaria section of they party. The second state co-chair still needs to be decided.

Aiwanger was found dead in a Berlin hotel room at the age of 55 with no foul play suspected. He's been the party's defining figure for almost four decades, having led the Free Voters to substantial success, especially in Bavaria.

The Free Voters are originally a grass roots party in Bavaria and sit on the conservative edge of the political spectrum. They've been in government in Bavaria as junior coaltion partners of the Christian Social Union (CSU), sister party to Chancellor Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

There are also changes in the Bavarian state government. Tobias Gotthardt is to take over as economy minister, while Environment Minister Thorsten Glauber is set to become deputy premier behind Bavaria state Premier Markus Söder. The appointments still require formal approval by party conventions.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has inisted that NATO was ready to defend itself in the face of potential Russian threats against any of its member states.

"We will always defend every inch of our NATO territory," Wadephul said at the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.

His comments come after three Russian projectiles violated Polish airspace on Friday and crashed in the southeast of the country.

Wadephul is attending the NATO assembly in Berlin and DW has   a dedicated blog on those talks  where you can read all about how Russia's war in Ukraine is taking center stage for the defense alliance.

A massive strike is underway in Germany hitting major car brands another manufacturing factors. Metal and electrical workers are demanding better pay ahead of upcoming wage talks later this week. The strike has been initiated by IG Metall, Germany’s biggest and most powerful union.

Famous car brands Mercedes and BMW  were affected as was an Opel plant, which is part of the international Stellantis group.

The strikes began on Friday and are due to continue until Tuesday. Wage negotiations are then set to continue on Wednesday with another round of collective bargaining for some 3.7 million workers across the sector.

The union is demanding a pay rise of 5% over one year while the employers association, Gesamtmetall, has offered a one-time payment and a pay increase of 1.3%.

The tough struggle over wages comes as especially the German car industry is facing serious headwinds because of higher energy prices, US tariffs and mounting Chinese competition.

A German investigative media report published on Monday claims that Russia would be able to launch a nuclear-armed satellite, called Sputnik-S, into orbit within the space of about 60 days if it wished.

The report from public broadcasters WDR, NDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, cites a warning from German and other western intelligence agencies that it says was circulated at the start of November.

It said that a launch "could" take place by December, without quoting the document or clarifying whether it was talking only about a Russian capability, or a more firm intention.

The report said the satellite itself had been built several years ago and was being stored in the Moscow area.

German authorities did not respond to requests for comment on the record while the Russian Embassy in Berlin said the claims were part of a "propaganda" campaign.

The report matches longstanding warnings, mainly but not exclusively from the US, that Russia could be preparing a nuclear strike in Earth orbit designed to take out a large number of satellites.

This could have a severe impact on intelligence, communications, logisticts, navigation and other key services.

Russia's war in Ukraine, and the Ukrainian military's reliance on the Starlink satellite internet service, has provided an additional reminder of the strategic significance of satellites in orbit.

German exports to Africa have reached a new record. That’s according to a fresh study just as the country's president embarks on a trip to several African countries.

Exports are expected to rise by 6% in 2026 to reach about 30 billion euros ($33bn).

What’s behind the growing demand are especially orders from South Africa, Egypt, Tunisia, Nigeria, Angola and Kenya — countries where inflation has been dropping and exchange rates are more stable.

The biggest single export at the moment is a high-speed train network to Egypt. Other main exports include electrical equipment, optical instruments, plastics and pharmaceuticals, as well as food products, including dairy goods, cereals and baked goods.

The data is being reported by the Reuters news agency, based on the government-owned agency Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI), which promotes foreign trade and investment in Germany.

In 2025, exports to Africa had risen by 8% while in 2024 it had gone down.

The Germangovernment has blamed oil and gas-producing nations for the COP climate conference ending without an agreement.

"The oil and gas industry is still dragging its feet," German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said after the UN climate talks had failed on Sunday. "Some oil-producing nations realize that the situation is becoming serious for them — that is why they are blocking it so vehemently," saidSchneider.

Almost two days into overtime, the COP31 climate talks in Turkey ended on Sunday as many countries, including the EU, rejected a final declaration.

Major sticking points at the summit included a commitment to accelerate global electrification and whether or not to explicitly mention plans to phase out fossil fuels. The suggested final declaration put forward by the COP presidency did not mention fossil fuels and according to critics would have undermined the shift away from fossil fuels.

"I understand that this poses a threat to the business model of those countries that sell us oil and gas. But electrification will make the world a more peaceful and stable place," Schneider said.

The inability to agree on a final declaration comes as climate change is increasingly linked to worsening heatwaves, floods and other natural catastrophes.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier begins a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya with a focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers.

He begins in Abidjan, where he is due to meet Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara. Steinmeier will also visit a vocational college and the International Academy for Counter-Terrorism before travelling on to Ghana.

In the capital Accra on Tuesday, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa."

His final stop will be Kenya, where he will meet President William Ruto in Nairobi on Wednesday.

The German president is traveling with a German business delegation and wants to encourage closer economic ties and greater investment in Africa.

The trip is his 11th to sub-Saharan Africa and his final one as president as his term in office due to end next March.

#655. JPMorgan Chase says temporary software bug is affecting consumer banking

JPMorgan Chase reported a "technical issue" that was affecting some consumer banking services Monday.

The bank said a "temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" was causing some customer transactions to take longer than usual, though it said customers can still access their accounts and funds.

"There is no evidence it is cyber-related," a JPMorgan spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC.

"This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," the spokesperson said. "We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today."

CNBC's Eamon Javers reported there was no indication of bad actors involved.

Still, other major banks were listed in outage reports as transactions between Chase and other institutions appeared to get held up. Users reported errors as early as 11:30 a.m. ET.

A representative for U.S. Bank said that company was "not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays."

Zelle is the peer-to-peer payments system backed by many of the largest U.S. banks, including JPMorgan.

The outage reports come days after separate, widespread issues with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers.

— CNBC's Leslie Picker contributed to this report.

#654. ‘Club Kid’ Star Reggie Absolom on His Friendship With Jordan Firstman and Missing Out on a ‘Harry Potter’ Role: ‘J.K. Rowling Is a No Anyway’

Walking the red carpet at the Cannes Film Festival and receiving a seven-minute standing ovation is an emotional event for anyone — but especially when you’re 14, and it’s your first time acting in a feature film. Such was the case for “Club Kid” star Reggie Absolom. But Absolom was determined to appear as cool, calm and collected as the blue waters of the Mediterranean Sea.

“Jordan Firstman was on my left, Cara Delevingne was on my right, and I was crying so much,” Absolom tells Variety about standing through the applause that followed the film’s premiere screening. “The first thing Cara says to me, she looks at me and goes, ‘I know you were crying,’ because I was trying to hold the tears because I knew cameras were on me.” Related Stories Denis Villeneuve Was ‘Deeply Disappointed’ When Disney Put ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ on Same Release Date as ‘Dune 3’: ‘I Hope We Will Survive’ Luca Guadagnino Wants Next Movie to Be a 'Love Story,' Confirms 'American Psycho’ and 'Separate Rooms’ Not Happening

Despite the crowd’s cheers, it wasn’t until Absolom found out that A24 (his preference, “because they do pretty good things for indie movies”) had outmaneuvered the competition (with a whopping bid of $17 million) that he fully realized, “OK, people like this film.”

That’s a little bit of an understatement. “Club Kid” was nominated for best feature at the Gothams and has delivered impressive box office numbers since its limited release on Nov. 6; in its second week in theaters, Firstman’s film tallied an impressive $28,002 per-screen average. To date, “Club Kids” has grossed more than $5 million globally.

In the film, Absolom plays Arlo, the 10-year-old son of a washed-up party promoter named Peter (Firstman), whose excessive drug habits end his tenure running New York City’s queer nightlife scene. When Arlo shows up on his father’s doorstep, they are both forced to grow up and figure out how to navigate the rest of their lives.

The teenage British actor won the role after auditioning for HBO’s upcoming “Harry Potter” series. Absolom reached the final stage of auditions to join the wizarding world, but didn’t get the job. So, U.K. casting director Lucy Bevan mentioned him to her fellow casting director Carmen Cuba, who had been searching for the perfect youngster to play Arlo. Aside from the fact that both boys are British, Absolom and his character seem to have quite a bit in common.

“I love to get good at things,” Absolom says, listing the similarities between himself and Arlo, whose artistic aspirations are focused on DJing, instead of acting. “Obviously, getting there is a bit annoying, because I want to be good at everything the first time I try it. But even if I’m not, I will keep doing it until I am good at it.”

Read on to find out how a potential 10 years in Hogwarts turned into 26 days immersed in New York City’s indie sleaze scene, what Absolom learned from filming his first major movie and how he’s processing the Oscar buzz.

I don’t remember the exact words, but someone told me that having this performance as a kid shows that I will only get better. And someone told me that this is one of the performances of the year. That meant loads.

Josh Hutcherson. He was with Jordan in New York. He sat behind me in the screening, and he seemed like he was really enjoying it.

I mean, they’re pretty fun. I don’t stay for ages because I like to get myself a good night’s sleep, but I walk around, talk to people a bit, maybe have some Diet Coke or something like that. But they’re pretty fun. The music’s actually always pretty good.

I DJed in London, which was really fun. It’s a really cool club because you have to walk through this fully graffitied-up tunnel to get to it.

I learned during the movie, with Saturn Risin9. In the scene where she’s teaching me, she’s actually teaching me how to do things.

I mean, not like Peter or anything like that. I won’t be going weekly. Maybe once every month or two with a good group of friends could be fun.

The fact that he can let out so much emotion all at once. And then the next day, he wants to be such a good son, so he makes Jordan the playlist that they can add to together because he really wants to be a good kid so much, even though his parents before weren’t so good to him.

“Sex with Me” by Rihanna. That was on the top. I remember that. Basically, all the songs that are in the film. There were a few more songs that when I first listened to them, I was like, “Oh, I’m not sure.” Now I’m like, “Oh my God, some of these are my favorite songs.”

He seemed like a really kind guy, and the directions that he gave me during the auditions were really easy to understand and really easy to accomplish. So, I was really happy that I might be able to work with a director who can give me simple, easy-to-understand directions, instead of using big words in a direction that aren’t needed when you could just put it simpler. [It] will just make it harder for the actor to do it because they might be overthinking it. That’s what he never wanted anyone to do: overthink doing the lines. He just said, “Just do it how you would.”

We are super good friends after this whole press tour. This has only strengthened our bond, because we would have such random conversations and laugh about the stupidest things on set, like memes that we found on TikTok that we both know and we still do. There are so many things, so many references that we’ll say to each other that we just laugh about way too much before an interview. I bet there’s some interviews that are out there where we’re holding back laughter at the very beginning because we had just said something really stupid before the person walked in.

The first day is blocked out of my memory because all I remember is the second day, which is the throwing-up scene. Second day, and they make me throw up on camera. Not a good first impression.

The pizza that we ate was nice. It was pretty good, but then they had to blend it up with applesauce. It was cold but also warm; it was lumpy as hell, and it kind of stank too. There was a cup of it next to me because I had to drink it just before. Record, “Action!” And then they were like, “Wait, wait, wait! We need to move the slide.” I was like, “I have it in my mouth, guys. Hurry up!” And then I swear, I wish someone had taken a photo of me after every take to see how the color drained from my face because I was genuinely gonna be sick if I didn’t take a break. After the third take, I was like, “Guys, give me a break. I’m sitting outside. Just give me a second.”

I hadn’t been on set for that long — to the point where I’d been around adults for five weeks straight, not talking to kids. I had a PlayStation in my apartment so I would play with my friends. I would talk to them, and I could act like a kid because I wasn’t just around adults.

The music taste has to be one. But Arlo also seems like he wants to be, like, a really good DJ and he really wants to be good at skateboarding. And I love to be good. I love to get good at things. Obviously, getting there is a bit annoying because I want to be good at everything the first time I try it. But even if I’m not, I will keep doing it until I am good at it.

Because I used to play football, like what you call soccer [Absolom puts on an American accent], and on the way, because my dad was driving me, he played “Freak on a Leash” by Korn. I was like, “OK, this is making me feel something that I’ve never felt before.” It was like anger, but good anger. It was weird. But then I was like, “OK, I need to get more of this in my playlist” and I deleted all the ’90s and 2000s rap that I had in my playlist, swapped it out for metal and then recently swapped it out for Cocteau Twins.

Cocteau Twins. Part Time. You heard of them? No? No one has. It says they have 300,000 monthly listeners and I haven’t met a single one of them. Pinback. Earth, Wind and Fire. The song that’s like “the 21st night of September.”

OK! Yeah, Jordan and I have one. [The pair’s collaborative playlist was released on Spotify.]

Well, I feel like they go out somewhere, Oscar, Peter, Arlo, as a family, kind of. I don’t know where they would go. Where’s a place that they’d all like to go? I feel like Nicky (Eldar Isgandarov) and Evelyn (Colleen Camp) are there for some reason. I feel like they want to tag along because maybe they just have a day out. Maybe they go to Times Square or something for a day. And then I feel like just Arlo and Peter go to a record store again.

That no matter what’s happened to you, if you’ve had maybe a bad year, maybe you’ve had a bad few years, you’ve still got your whole life ahead of you. Don’t throw it away just because of the few bad years that you’ve had.

Oh my gosh! I’d be happy if we got nominated for one award, no matter how big it is. I’d be so happy if I got nominated for any award. Obviously, winning is a humongous bonus, but I’d just be happy to be there and experience it. Winning isn’t the most important thing, but it would be fun. I like to win.

Definitely bringing my mom, of course, because she’s like my [personal assistant] as well as my mom. Definitely bring my dad too. How many plus-ones do I get? I think my sister would want to come, maybe just to be in the place. Maybe not so much for me, but she would want to come for me and to see it. Probably just my real close family and one of my aunts because she is obsessed. She’s like, “Can I chaperone you? Can I come with you?” I feel like I’d bring her because she’s obsessed with New York, and I feel like she’d love L.A. as well.

I just want to do new stuff, like anything that comes to me, really. So, like, I’m not 100% sure what will come next.

“Harry Potter” is out the window. “Harry Potter” got me here, and I thank it for that. But I think we don’t worry about it anymore.

I’d rather do this. “Harry Potter” would have been a cool set to be on because it would have looked cool, but there would have been so many more people; I wouldn’t have gotten to bond with everyone. I loved everyone on this set. I had such a good time filming it, and I think J.K. Rowling’s a no anyway, but Jordan is a big yes.

#653. ‘A Girl Unknown,’ ‘Crawling Into Myself,’ ‘Concrete Land’ Take Main Prizes at Doha Film Festival

Zou Jing’s “A Girl Unknown,” Asmahan Bkerat’s “Concrete Land” and Hamad Al-Fayhani’s “Crawling Into Myself” won the top prizes at the sophomore edition of the revamped Doha Film Festival, which took place between Nov. 19-27 in the Qatari capital.

The Doha Film Festival has transformed the Doha Film Institute’s existing Ajyal Film Festival, dedicated to youth and family-friendly cinema, into a more ambitious international event for a broader audience. Prizes totaled over $300,000 across four competition strands: international feature film competition, short film competition, the Ajyal film competition (judged by the festival’s youth jury), and the Made in Qatar competition, dedicated to projects made in Qatar regardless of the director’s provenance. Related Stories Producer of Oscar-Nominated ‘A Friend Of Dorothy’ to Make Directorial Debut With Disability Drama ‘Hidden Creatures,’ Easyjet Founder Boards as EP (EXCLUSIVE) What’s New on Disney+ in December 2026

“A Girl Unknown,” which won Best Narrative Feature in International Competition, trails a young Chinese girl passed between three families between the ages of 6 and 18; “Crawling Into Myself,” the winner of the Made in Qatar competition, tells the story of a man grappling with a rare illness that erases his facial features. “Concrete Land,” the Best Documentary in International Competition, is a multi-generational portrait of a mixed-race family fighting displacement and hostility in Jordan.

Fatma Hassan Alremaihi, festival director and CEO of the Doha Film Institute, said: “Tonight, as we celebrate the winners of the 2026 Doha Film Festival, we celebrate far more than cinematic achievement. We recognize the power of stories to transcend borders, challenge perspectives and bring the experiences of people and communities into the global conversation.”

The festival director added that the Doha Film Institute “believes that important voices deserve to be seen, heard and recognized.”

“The Doha Film Festival exists to provide that platform—bringing together filmmakers and audiences from across the world, championing bold and independent storytelling, and creating space for stories that might otherwise go untold,” she added. “The films we honor tonight remind us that cinema is not simply a reflection of the world we live in; it is a force that can shape how we understand it, connect with one another and imagine a more empathetic future.”

This year’s jury at the Qatari festival was presided over by Japanese director Naomi Kawase, who chose the winners alongside French Tunisian actor Adam Bessa, Tunisian producer Dora Bouchoucha, Italian documentary filmmaker Gianfranco Rosi and award-winning Palestinian filmmaker and artist Kamal Aljafari.

The short film competition jury was presided over by French Moroccan producer Karim Aitouna, who was joined by Malaysian filmmaker Amanda Nell Eu, and Swiss-Rwandan actress and filmmaker Kayije Kagame. The Made in Qatar jury was led by Lebanese actress and filmmaker Yumna Marwan along with Qatari filmmaker Al Johara Al Thani and Palestinian Belgian filmmaker and producer Naël Khleifi.

The ceremony, which was hosted by Sudanese filmmaker and presenter Amjad Al-Nour, was attended by names such as Elia Suleiman, Brigitte Lacombe and Ahmed Al Baker. Other notable guests included H.E. Sheikha Al-Mayassa bint Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, chairperson of DFI; H.E. Sheikh Dr. Abdulla bin Ali Al Thani, managing director and vice chairman of the board of directors of Qatar Leadership Centre; Hamad Omar Al-Mannai, chief executive officer of Media City Qatar; and Eng. Abdulaziz Ali Al Mawlawi, chief executive officer of Visit Qatar.

Earlier in the week, the festival delivered a successful industry sidebar, the Doha Industry Days. The three-day event was attended by some 450 prominent executives from 38 countries. Speakers included “Squid Game” creator Hwang Dong-hyuk, “Avengers” director Joe Russo, Omar Sy and Noomi Rapace. The buzzy Industry Days saw the announcement of several projects, including a Neon-backed biopic titled “Caesar” about Syrian military officer Farid Al-Madhhan and two other biopics, one on Egyptian music star Mohamed Mounir and the other on Lebanese pop star Fadel Shaker.

#652. Postcards from your graves

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Wendy Nikel is a speculative-fiction author with a degree in elementary education, a fondness for road trips and a terrible habit of forgetting where she’s left her cup of tea. For more info, visit wendynikel.com.

You send me postcards from your graves, but by the time they reach me, you’re gone.

1) Quoted in Peculiar Letters from the Western Front, which I’d borrowed from the library the day before you left:

I’ve figured it out, B. The failsafe implanted in my wrist must have been misprogrammed. I never should have let AI help me write the code. Instead of pulling me back to the present whenever I’m in danger, for some reason, it keeps sending me into danger. (AI always has trouble with prepositions, doesn’t it?) Gotta go; they’re bombing again. Love, T.

The machine hums in the corner of the lab where you left it. “Just a quick test trip!” I keep hearing you say, your final words caught in a loop in my mind.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

2) Delivered via Western Union, water-stained and faded, with instructions to hold for delivery until the present day:

Aloha, B. You’ll never guess where I ended up! Hawaii! A bit of a detour from “two weeks ago” (I swear, I entered it correctly! The machine must have some bugs to work out!) I’ll write again with the exact date as soon as I can find a newspaper, but it must be the early ’40s. Lots of war talk among the men stationed here. Love, T.

I plot them all out like a madman, connecting dates and places and all the catastrophes that conspire to keep us apart. I haunt disaster sites, archives and museums, searching for clues for my collection, as if completing the puzzle might bring you back.

3) Scratched onto a lifeboat oar at the Titanic museum:

Happened again, B. Not much time before the you-know-what. Wanted you to know I was here. T.

4) Sharpied discreetly on The Sphere by Fritz Koenig, displayed at Liberty Park, New York:

I hate knowing what’s coming, B. I want to warn these people. Would they even believe me if I did? T.

5) Printed in the editorial section of a 1900 newspaper:

This cryptic telegram, addressed to our editor on Sept. 8th, was the last to arrive from Galveston before the recent storm.

Please print the following in your newspaper, word for word.

“B. Trip to Hawaii was a disaster. Infamously. Zeroes got me. Somehow ended up here. Trying to figure out how to get back to you before the storm hits. Love, T.”

I am the one who’s filled our home with history, while you’ve lived your life in dogged pursuit of the future. Is it ironic, then, that you’re there, in those places I know so well, while I’m stuck here, trying to sort out what happens next?

6) From a note scribbled in the communion ledger of St Michael’s Church, Old Town, Chicago:

B — I think it’s the large language model. Like fire, it follows the path of least resistance, the most well-worn ruts in the road. What rut is more worn in the road of time-travel stories than experiencing, preventing, observing disasters? And what disasters are more well-worn than these? T.

#651. NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos

"The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges."

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

When DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an important part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit

Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

The experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact

After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

"Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!"

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

Materials provided by European Space Agency (ESA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

When humans live on the moon, we'll need to grow food on the moon, too.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon. The space agency even plans to build a moon base for its astronauts to call home. But humans living inside lunar habitats around the clock will need three square meals a day, so researchers have been working on how to grow food on the moon.

To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results. The researchers published their findings Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal.

"We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in a statement. "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon."

To grow the spuds, the scientists used five different materials that are similar to regolith, the dust and rocks that cover the moon's surface. The moon contains various regions with unique surface makeups, so the materials they used simulated regolith from both lunar mare and lunar highland regions.

The secret ingredient was vermicompost, a soil that's rich in nutrients. The team added different levels of vermicompost to the simulated regolith to grow the potatoes. They figured out that fake regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as growing potatoes with regular soil.

"We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab, said in the same statement.

The idea is that astronauts in the future could bring a little nutrient-rich soil with them and mix it with regolith to grow potatoes. After all, it'd cost a ton to ship all that food from Earth.
